item.content:encoded:
BOSTON – No one really knew what the road back to the field would look like for Alex Bregman in the immediate aftermath of the scary scene on Sunday in Cincinnati. The Cubs’ star third baseman was struck in the left side of the face by a foul ball and sustained multiple fractures, making his well-being the biggest concern.
On Friday morning at Fenway Park, Bregman’s name was back in the lineup for the Cubs, who slotted the veteran in as the designated hitter in the lineup’s third spot. Given the initial shock of his injury, having Bregman back so soon came not only as a relief, but as a potential boost as Chicago nears a National League Wild Card Series.
“It’s incredible,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said.
The Cubs understand there is risk involved with having Bregman return to the lineup less than a week removed from the incident, but the third baseman went through multiple days of workouts and was cleared by the team’s doctors. After Bregman showed no concussion symptoms, passed vision testing and was deemed not to require surgery, Friday was circled as a possible target for his comeback.
Bregman began with tracking pitches against the high-velocity Trajekt machine at Wrigley Field on Tuesday and advanced to hitting on Wednesday. By Thursday, the third baseman was out in the field going through running drills to test how that felt. And as the Cubs celebrated their postseason clinch on Thursday night, Bregman stayed to the side at his locker, protected from the fray by plastic sheeting hanging in the locker room.
Counsell noted that Bregman was “itching to get in” Thursday’s clincher against the Marlins.
“There were a lot of unknowns,” Counsell said. “It was a freak injury. It’s an injury that we don’t deal with very often, that you don’t experience very often, so you’re kind of unaware of the risk and things like that. There are risks. And we’ve talked to Alex about that, but I think we’ve done the best we can to minimize them and just move forward.”
Bregman was waiting on deck at Great American Ball Park on Sunday, when Michael Busch checked his swing and fouled off a pitch from Reds pitcher Luis Mey in the fourth inning. Bregman had little time to react and immediately grabbed at his face and headed down the tunnel before being taken to a local hospital.
A staffer remained in Cincinnati to drive Bregman back to Chicago and the third baseman posted a photo on Instagram of his bruised, bloodied face with his left eye swollen shut. The swelling reduced significantly in the days leading up to the trip to Boston and Bregman planned on wearing a modified helmet to help guard against any setbacks.
In that social media post, Bregman declared, “I’ll be back,” and he delivered faster on that promise than fans might have expected.
Counsell said Bregman’s personality and drive to stay on the field have made an impact on the Cubs this season.
“Look, Alex’s best trait is just, the man loves baseball,” Counsell said. “And he’s super competitive. And he’s relentless in his pursuit to be a little bit better. And so, that just rubs off on people. And he talks about it non-stop. I mean, every one of us has gotten late-night texts or observations, so it’s great.
“And it makes you love it, and it makes you want to go to battle with him.”
While Pete Crow-Armstrong has emerged as the NL’s favorite to take home the MVP Award, Bregman has also turned in the type of season that should get down-ballot consideration. Through 153 games, Bregman had 5.2 fWAR with 26 homers, 32 doubles, 89 RBIs and an .804 OPS to go along with Gold Glove-caliber defense. He has really taken off since the All-Star break, posting a .978 OPS.
And with his return to the lineup, Bregman is on the cusp of playing in the postseason for a 10th consecutive season.
“His relentlessness is infectious,” Counsell said.

item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners have had a rough 2026 season. After coming one win shy of the World Series a year ago, they've failed to make the postseason despite the AL West leader having a record under .500 with three games to go.
This Mariners season is one of the worst in recent years due to the expectations coming into the season. A lot of people are to blame, but one of the main reasons why things fell apart is thanks to Cal Raleigh.
Jayson Stark of The Athletic named Raleigh the American League's "LVP" or "Least Valuable Player." Instead of Vladimir Guerrero Jr. earning this label for his poor 2026 season, Raleigh is the LVP of the season for a few key reasons.
Why Cal Raleigh earned LVP award over Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
"The Mariners' catcher has gone from MVP runner-up, 60-homer machine and heartbeat of a team that was eight outs from the World Series to... eh, hoo boy," Stark writes. "The Big Dumper has been worth 1.1 WAR all season, according to Baseball Reference..."
Raleigh's drop-off this season isn't limited to just some struggles to accumulate bWAR. There is so much else that's gone wrong for the Mariners catcher.
"But would that alone have been enough to push Raleigh 'ahead' of Vladdy in this LVP derby? It would not," Stark writes. "To pull that off would have taken one of the steepest drop-offs, from one season to the next, in baseball history. Unfortunately for Raleigh, that's what he's enduring."
Raleigh has gone from 60 homers to 23 with three games to go. That's the biggest drop-off of all-time for a 60-homer hitter, according to Stark.
Regarding his 1.1 bWAR, Stark shared, "And if you're wondering how many top-two MVP finishers have ever gone from at least 7.0 that year to under 2. 0the next, that would be none -- until now."
Raleigh's drop-off in homers and bWAR is something baseball has never seen before. But it's so much more than just those two poor statistics.
He posted a slash line of .247/.359/.589 last season. In 2026, his average dropped 68 points, his on-base percentage 63 points, and his slugging percentage an astounding 220 points with three games to go.
Those numbers will look different by the end of the season, but those are some truly terrible drop-offs, even if he were to get hot in these final three games of 2026.
Going from a 169 OPS+ to a 92 OPS+, and a .948 OPS to a .663 OPS, is an all-time fall-off for any player in MLB history.
All of that is exceptionally terrible production, but considering Guerrero has just nine homers this season with a .695 OPS and a 92 OPS+, he's not the "LVP" this season due to the sheer drop-off from Raleigh in 2025 to 2026.
It's not just the drop-off for Raleigh that's playing a role here either. The Blue Jays had a rough 2026 season, but they at least played better than Seattle did this year.
Raleigh is the "LVP" of the American League in 2026 thanks to the record-breaking drop-off he's had from 2025 to 2026.
While he might not be the worst player in the AL, his production in 2026 is far below what was expected of him this season and is more than deserving of the "Least Valuable Player" label this year.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Diamondbacks' Ketel Marte gets dubious 'LVP' label from MLB analyst | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: The Arizona Diamondbacks are fighting for a postseason spot, with only the Philadelphia Phillies within reach heading into the final few days of the regular season. There are a lot of players who've helped the Diamondbacks get to this point, but they have also dealt with others who've held the team back, whether it's due to an injury or poor play. Or, in the case of Jayson Stark of The Athletic's "LVP" in the NL for the 2026 season, Ketel Marte, it's off-field drama and underwhelming at-best pro
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Diamondbacks are fighting for a postseason spot, with only the Philadelphia Phillies within reach heading into the final few days of the regular season.
There are a lot of players who've helped the Diamondbacks get to this point, but they have also dealt with others who've held the team back, whether it's due to an injury or poor play.
Or, in the case of Jayson Stark of The Athletic's "LVP" in the NL for the 2026 season, Ketel Marte, it's off-field drama and underwhelming at-best production. Marte was named by Stark as the "Least Valuable Player" in the NL for the 2026 season.
Ketel Marte called NL's 'LVP' for 2026 season
Marte earned Stark's LVP nomination for the National League thanks to a few different problems he's been a part of this season.
One of the biggest, most glaring issues for Marte was his unexpected absence from the team during their series against the Boston Red Sox.
He left the team on his own, was placed on the restricted list, and was seen in the casino late at night, not far from where his Diamondbacks' teammates were playing that same night.
Unfortunately, it's not just that whole debacle that explains why Marte is the Least Valuable Player in the NL this season, according to Stark.
"... Marte's on-base percentage is down more than 60 points from last year ... and his slugging percentage has dropped by over 80 points -- and his wRC+ (102) tells us he is basically just a league-average player, after two straight years in which he was about 50 percent better than league average. Not good," Stark writes.
Marte has posted 2.3 bWAR this season in 138 games played, hitting .250 with a .316 on-base percentage and a .435 slugging percentage.
His .893 OPS from the 2025 season has dropped considerably to a .752 OPS this season. That's a 141-point drop over one year.
Marte went from being a superstar who could carry the Diamondbacks if needed to just being a slightly above-average player.
While Marte hasn't been terrible, his off-field drama combined with a major offensive regression has made it clear that Marte has been a major disappointment this season.
Stark named him the NL's "Least Valuable Player" for the 2026 season. It's an unfortunate label, one that he's earned after quite the tumultuous 2026 season.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Julio Rodríguez Apologizes to Mariners Fans, but This Failure Goes Far Beyond Him
item.dc:creator: Tremayne Person; Unknown
item.description: Julio Rodríguez blasted a baseball 451 feet Thursday night. Earlier in the day, the Texas Rangers had eliminated the Mariners from postseason contention before they could take the field. Rodríguez still briefly gave them a lead with the second-longest home run of his career. Then Seattle surrendered it, lost 6-4 to an Angels team approaching 100 defeats and recorded its 85th loss of the season. There might not be a better snapshot of the 2026 Mariners. The talent remained visible. But winning ba
item.content:encoded:
Julio Rodríguez blasted a baseball 451 feet Thursday night. Earlier in the day, the Texas Rangers had eliminated the Mariners from postseason contention before they could take the field. Rodríguez still briefly gave them a lead with the second-longest home run of his career. Then Seattle surrendered it, lost 6-4 to an Angels team approaching 100 defeats and recorded its 85th loss of the season.
There might not be a better snapshot of the 2026 Mariners. The talent remained visible. But winning baseball just wasn’t in the cards. Rodríguez stood in front of the Mariners logo afterward and apologized directly to the fans. He thanked them for sticking around through a season that began with World Series expectations and ended without another postseason run.
He did the right thing. But it shouldn’t be the final word from this organization.
A Down Year at the Plate Was Only Part of the Problem
Rodríguez had a disappointing season. Entering September 25, he’s slashed .250/.311/.407 with 22 home runs and 70 RBIs in 148 games. It’s not awful, but that doesn’t meet the standard he established or the expectations attached to him. His defense has slipped even more dramatically. After producing 11 Outs Above Average in 2025, Rodríguez sat at -3 following Thursday’s game, the first negative OAA season of his career.
That belongs in the discussion. Rodríguez is not exempt because he is likable, marketable or capable of crushing a baseball. The Mariners needed their franchise players to be better.
Seattle entered Friday ranked last in total defensive value at -46.6, roughly five runs below the Athletics. A team doesn’t reach the bottom of baseball because its center fielder had a down year. It takes poor personnel fits, sloppy execution and standards that were either not enforced or not effective.
Cal Raleigh called the season a “collective failure.” He pointed to a lack of focus, execution and energy before saying the Mariners didn’t deserve to make the playoffs. Bryan Woo spoke about disappointment, anger, sadness and embarrassment. The players have supplied honesty and accountability for their disappointing season. Now the microphone needs to turn toward the people responsible for deciding what comes next.
Jerry Dipoto and Justin Hollander constructed this roster. Dan Wilson and his staff were responsible for its daily preparation and on-field standards. Ownership determines whether those same decision-makers receive another opportunity to repair what went wrong. Every layer owns a piece of this. And that’s why this is a collective failure.
Some fans responded to Rodríguez’s apology by calling for postgame conditioning or another form of visible punishment. It sounds impulsive, but we understand how exhausting this season has been to watch. The 2026 Mariners have made everyone want to see somebody run until the lights go out. But that is punishment, not accountability. Accountability comes through decisions. Plus, these are adults who should be more than capable of policing themselves.
The Mariners needed urgency months ago. They needed to clean up their defensive lapses, a stronger identity and fewer nights spent relearning lessons a contender should already understand. Their offseason response must include an honest evaluation of their coaching staff, roster additions that improve the offense without making the defense worse and enough depth that one injury or regression doesn’t pull the floor out from under the entire season.
Waiting for Rodríguez, Raleigh, Josh Naylor and the rotation to return to their best forms isn’t an offseason plan. It is another wager on everything breaking correctly. Rodríguez should arrive in 2027 determined to restore his standing as one of baseball’s best two-way players. That’s his responsibility.
The Mariners owe him and their fans something larger: a team that doesn’t require the best possible version of Julio Rodríguez simply to function.
Tremayne Person is the Publisher for Mariners On SI and the Site Expert at Friars on Base, with additional bylines across FanSided’s MLB division. He founded the Keep It Electric podcast in 2023 and covers baseball with a blend of analysis, context, and a little well-timed side-eye just to keep things honest. Tremayne grew up a Mariners fan in Richmond, Va., and that passion ultimately led him to move to Seattle to cover the team closely and become a regular at home games. Through his writing, he connects with fans who want a deeper, more personal understanding of the game. When he’s not at T-Mobile Park, he’s with his dog, gaming, or finding the next storyline worth digging into.
Follow TremaynePerson

item.title: [PHILADELPHIA.Today] Why the Phillies Built Their Lineup Around Schwarber and Arraez
item.dc:creator: Jensen Toussaint
item.description: The Phillies have turned baseball’s oldest lineup blueprint upside down, and the runs are following, writes Jared Diamond for The Wall Street Journal. Since reshaping the batting order, Philadelphia has raised its scoring from 4.39 to 4.67 runs per game, jumping from 16th to ninth in MLB. For generations, the formula barely changed: a high-contact table-setter hit near the top and the biggest power bat hit in the middle. The Phillies have flipped the script. Kyle Schwarber, one of baseball’s mos
item.content:encoded:
The Phillies have turned baseball’s oldest lineup blueprint upside down, and the runs are following, writes Jared Diamond for The Wall Street Journal.
Since reshaping the batting order, Philadelphia has raised its scoring from 4.39 to 4.67 runs per game, jumping from 16th to ninth in MLB.
For generations, the formula barely changed: a high-contact table-setter hit near the top and the biggest power bat hit in the middle.
The Phillies have flipped the script.
Kyle Schwarber, one of baseball’s most feared home-run hitters and also one of its most frequent strikeout victims, now leads off.
Batting cleanup — the spot long reserved for sluggers like Lou Gehrig and Joe DiMaggio — is Luis Arraez, a three-time batting champion with little home-run power who hits behind Bryce Harper.
With the Giants, before Philadelphia acquired him at the trade deadline, Arraez typically batted first or second.
Even manager Don Mattingly acknowledged how strange the alignment would have looked during his playing days in the 1980s and 1990s.
“Things are changing,” Mattingly said.
Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski said that in an earlier era, a hitter with Arraez’s profile would have been penciled into one of the first two spots almost automatically.
Instead, Philadelphia wants his bat in play with runners aboard, where his .349 career average with runners in scoring position can do the most damage.
The logic is rather than forcing hitters into traditional roles, build the lineup around what each one does best.
As Dombrowski put it, “It does just tell you how the game has changed.”
Read more about how the Phillies are challenging 125 years of batting-order convention and why their upside-down approach is producing more runs in The Wall Street Journal.

item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: The MLB playoffs are approaching, and the Chicago Cubs have received a major boost with Alex Bregman set to return to the lineup Friday against his former team, the Boston Red Sox. Bregman has been sidelined since Sunday after suffering a facial fracture when he was hit by a foul ball while standing in the on-deck circle during Chicago's game against the Cincinnati Reds. Bregman returns to Cubs lineup Jun 27, 2026; Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA; Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (3) high-fives
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are approaching, and the Chicago Cubs have received a major boost with Alex Bregman set to return to the lineup Friday against his former team, the Boston Red Sox.
Bregman has been sidelined since Sunday after suffering a facial fracture when he was hit by a foul ball while standing in the on-deck circle during Chicago's game against the Cincinnati Reds.
Bregman returns to Cubs lineup
Jun 27, 2026; Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA; Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (3) high-fives his teammates after scoring a run against the Milwaukee Brewers in the sixth inning at American Family Field. Mandatory Credit: Michael McLoone-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Despite the injury, the two-time World Series champion is ready to return to action. Bregman will serve as the Cubs' designated hitter and bat third in Friday's lineup against Boston, while Matt Shaw will take over Bregman's usual position at third base.
The return is significant for a Cubs team preparing for the postseason. Before suffering the injury, the 32-year-old was enjoying a productive first season in Chicago, hitting .262/.352/.452 with 26 home runs and 89 RBI.
Bregman joined the Cubs as a free agent during the offseason after spending the previous season with the Red Sox. His return against Boston adds another storyline to an already important series.
Cubs race for playoff position
Chicago has already clinched a National League Wild Card spot, but there is still plenty to play for during the final series of the regular season.
The Cubs currently hold the second Wild Card position in the National League, sitting one game behind the San Diego Padres for the top spot. At the same time, Chicago is only one game ahead of the Philadelphia Phillies, who currently occupy the final playoff position.
That tight race means every game carries significant importance as the Cubs look to secure their postseason position. Having Bregman back in the lineup could provide Chicago with another experienced bat as the team prepares for October baseball.
Bregman and the Cubs will begin their final three-game series of the regular season Friday against the Red Sox. With Chicago battling for playoff positioning and Bregman returning from a facial fracture, the series could be an important final test before the postseason begins.
For the Cubs, getting one of their key players back at this stage of the season provides a welcome boost as they prepare for the challenges ahead.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] It's Over For Jackson Holliday With The Orioles. Even Mike Elias Has To Know It
item.dc:creator: Jason La Canfora; Unknown
item.description: The best time for baseball failure Mike Elias to trade one of his failing former top draft picks is, invariably right now. Because the longer they persist in his laughingstock player development strata – and the more they toil under what’s been a disaster medical and training staff - invariably their future value will decline and things will only get worse. Among Elias’s superpowers, wrecking top prospects is right up there with building third-grade rosters, hiring inane managers and constructin
item.content:encoded:
The best time for baseball failure Mike Elias to trade one of his failing former top draft picks is, invariably right now.
Because the longer they persist in his laughingstock player development strata – and the more they toil under what’s been a disaster medical and training staff - invariably their future value will decline and things will only get worse. Among Elias’s superpowers, wrecking top prospects is right up there with building third-grade rosters, hiring inane managers and constructing teams incapable of catching the ball or executing baseball fundamentals.
Which brings us to Jackson Holliday, Elias’s second first-overall selection (with his overt tank forcing even the craven and cynical billionaires who run baseball to change their draft rules), and why he needs to go this offseason. And to be clear Holliday needs to go ASAP as badly as Elias’s first overhyped first-overall pick, Adley Rutschman, needed to be jettisoned before the trade deadline. Long a Holliday skeptic myself – I begged and pleaded them to make him a cornerstone inn a Tarik Skubal package back in 2024 - I tried to keep an open mind that sweeping midseason stance and swing corrections might turn him around, but that was folly.
It’s time for him to be packaged (ideally with failed fifth-overall pick Colton Cowser as should have happened at the deadline) this winter.
This won’t get better here, and we have to operate now with the known constraints moving forward” Elias is as empowered as ever, overmatched puppet skipper Craig Albernaz is back for 2027, and the idea these mooks are going to turn Holliday into a winning centerfielder is ridiculous (though several top analysts believe it can be done). They couldn’t turn him into a competent second baseman after perpetual grifter Elias sold you he was a five-tool All Star shortstop when he drafted him.
Again, I watched him throughout the minors, called this out as an overhyped positionless prospect and begged them to sell him on him when the roster was a Skubal away from doing potential October damage. Alas, those days are gone and they’re not coming back.
Why Now?
So with the two-headed monster of Elibernaz (actually, let’s be real, it’s Albi-ass) coming back, and another Holliday offseason and/or spring training cut short due to surgery (pending wrist procedure) and him slight and brittle and unable to turn his natural speed into any kind of weapon and with him downright deficient at second base, he has to go.
With Jordan Westburg coming back from his latest surgery, and him brittle and not durable, but with a legit run-production profile this lineup desperately needs, he will be given every chance to bounce back. And at this point, I’m simplifying his program – Westburg is a second baseman. Less strain on the body there. Let’s get 120 games out of him there and some DH work.
Because we also know Elias is going to be all about Christian Encarnacion-Strand in 2027, loving to try to turn a AAAA guy into a regular, and with CES’s power productivity and the glove playing better than expected, he is in the mix. And Pete Alonso and Samuel Basallo block first base. Coby Mayo was the one young player who truly exceeded expectations on this roster, and he kills left-handed pitching and you can live with the glove at third once or twice a week.
And Gunnar Henderson is not an MLB shortstop and he won’t be here past the trade deadline and he could be dealt this winter (and they don’t have the guts to move him to third, where he’s always belonged). If he is dealt before the lockout, Blaze Alexander would be an option at short, and they should go get a glove-first shortstop anyway and stop running fake teams out there with no spine. Either way, Elias will want Alexander to play a lot, so you tell me where Holliday fits in?
What About Selling Low?
Never stopped Elias before, it’s another specialty of his, and it could always get worse. In Birdland, it always does. That's The Elias Way.
Holliday has too many voices in his head, and yet another new hitting staff that is surely on the way here as Elias scapegoats middle managers while being a 100% fraud himself, will only make it worse. I’m thinking his daddy is ready for him to have a fresh start (with a team further from alleged contention than the Orioles) and agent Scott Boras is ready for him to have a fresh start, where the pressure of being the overhyped 1-1 won’t matter as much.
We won’t belabor the point defensively, because it’s ugly all around and the instincts at 2B are not natural or fluid. He is 20th among all MLB players with at least 500 innings at second in fielding run value. He is in the 88th percentile in sprint speed and played nearly 100 games this season and had eight steals and got thrown out three times; in an era where they made stealing bases easier than ever, he has 29 steals to 14 times caught stealing for his career.
Abject failure they couldn’t fix this, but a smart organization probably can.
As for the hit tool, man, it’s still a mess. You could tell me he’ll still only be 23 by spring training, but he has 1100 MLB plate appearances and he’s also been in this org five years now and he is going backwards, rapidly. Injuries or not, he had a .640 OPS this season and he was 17 percent worse than the average MLB hitter (OPS+) … those are below his career totals (.654 OPS and 86 OPS+).
Holliday stopped swinging as hard and moved off the plate in the box and changed his swing plane in an effort to get on base more and work the ball between the gaps .. and ended up with a .300 OBP, much worse than last year, and a .229 average, also much worse than 2025. And really, the fact he ends the season on the IL like he began it, needing yet another procedure, kind of says it all.
He is a number nine hitter in a real MLB lineup, and I’m not sure where he plays most of the time. They gave him another run at the top of the lineup when he was hot in July, and that leadoff stint was largely a disaster (.267 OBP and .614 OPS). He had an amazing July, and arguably in every other month he looked like someone who needed more seasoning in AAA.
Holliday had a .582 OPS in 50 games at Camden Yards, a park that should suit him from the left side, and a .601 OPS in the second half of the season. It’s over here.
Sadly, it never even ever really got going here, and worst of all, the guy who created this problem is still the one charged with fixing it.

item.title: [NBC 5 Chicago] Alex Bregman back in Cubs lineup after suffering facial fractures from foul ball
item.dc:creator: James Neveau; Alex Dvorak
item.description: Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman is back in the lineup despite suffering multiple facial fractures after being hit by a foul ball last weekend. The Cubs listed Bregman as a designated hitter in the lineup for Game 1 of Friday's doubleheader with the Boston Red Sox. Bregman was standing near the on-deck circle during Sunday’s game against the Cincinnati Reds when Michael Busch hit a foul ball with a check swing. The ball hit Bregman just below his left eye. According to the Cubs, Bregman s
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman is back in the lineup despite suffering multiple facial fractures after being hit by a foul ball last weekend.
The Cubs listed Bregman as a designated hitter in the lineup for Game 1 of Friday's doubleheader with the Boston Red Sox.
Bregman was standing near the on-deck circle during Sunday’s game against the Cincinnati Reds when Michael Busch hit a foul ball with a check swing. The ball hit Bregman just below his left eye.
According to the Cubs, Bregman suffered multiple facial fractures, but the team did not put him on the injured list with just days left in the regular season. Bregman had been aiming to get back in the lineup in enough time to be ready for the playoffs. The Cubs clinched their spot in the playoffs Thursday with a win over the Marlins at Wrigley Field.
Bregman previously spoke to reporters and said despite his rough appearance, he was feeling fortunate the injury wasn’t worse.
“(I was) super lucky it hit where it hit and just a lot of gratitude that it wasn’t a few centimeters higher,” he said.
Manager Craig Counsell said he was happy with Bregman's progress so far.
Chicago Cubs
“He’s still got significant swelling in his face and his eye that needs to improve,” he said. “But all things considered, he’s in a good place.”
Bregman's addition to the lineup comes after the Cubs placed pitcher Edward Cabrera on the family medical emergency list, but details behind the designation were not immediately released. Gavin Hollowell was reinstated from the injury list in his place.
The Cubs' doubleheader with the Boston Red Sox Friday has seen multiple time changes so far as a looming nor'easter threatens the games through the weekend.
Earlier this week, officials announced Sunday's game with the Cubs would move to a 12:05 p.m. CT start on Friday afternoon. The two teams were then expected to play the second game of a split doubleheader beginning at 5:05 p.m. CT Friday.
But on Friday morning, the timing for the second game of the doubleheader changed 4:35 p.m. CT "due to potential weather impacts."

That means this is the final Friday night of the regular season that we can try to cash in on a few home run bets. There are three players I'm targeting to hit a dinger tonight, so let's dive into them.
Best MLB Home Run Bets Today

Kazuma Okamoto Home Run (+320)
Nick Lodolo gets the start for the Cincinnati Reds on Friday night, and he has had an issue giving up home runs this season, allowing 1.74 home runs per nine innings pitched. With that in mind, let's bet on Kazuma Okamoto, the Blue Jays' home run leader, to hit one more dinger this season. If you're going to bet on Jose Altuve to hit a home run, you should do it when the Astros are facing a left-handed pitcher. He has a .441 slugging percentage against lefties, compared to a .386 slugging percentage against righties. They'll face a lefty starter tonight in Jacob Lopez of the Athletics, who has allowed 1.69 home runs per nine innings pitched this season.

item.title: [Field Level Media] More work to do for Padres, Diamondbacks in regular season

Now San Diego has a chance to stay at home for the wild-card round of the National League playoffs — if it can take care of busines
item.content:encoded:
When the San Diego Padres were 50-53 going into a series in Miami on July 24, they were perhaps one more series loss away from being sellers at the MLB trade deadline.
Since then, they’ve posted the major leagues’ top record at 39-17, clinching their third straight playoff berth and their fifth in seven years with a 4-2 win Thursday night at the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Now San Diego has a chance to stay at home for the wild-card round of the National League playoffs — if it can take care of business in its final series of the season, starting Friday night against the Arizona Diamondbacks.
The Padres (89-70) are one game ahead of the Chicago Cubs for the first wild-card berth and two games ahead of the Philadelphia Phillies. They have won six straight series, mostly against sub-.500 teams, though they bookended it by taking two of three from the New York Yankees and the Dodgers.
“I think we learned a lot from those struggles,” Padres third baseman Manny Machado said. “Baseball’s a hard game, man, but we learned a lot from the struggles. To come in here and take a series from this team means a lot. We haven’t done that much lately.”
It marked the first time since April 2024 that San Diego has won a series at Dodger Stadium.
In the midst of a full-fledged celebration, center fielder Jackson Merrill sounded a cautionary note.
“We’ve still got three important games left,” he said.
The first of those will be pitched by Casey Mize (6-9, 3.96 ERA), who might be pitching for his spot on the wild-card roster. Mize was roughed up for five hits and five runs with five walks in three innings Saturday night during his team’s 7-6, 10-inning win over Miami.
Formerly with Detroit, Mize coughed up eight runs in 3 1/3 innings in his first start for the Padres in a 10-4 loss on Aug. 5 at Arizona.
As for the Diamondbacks (85-74), they flew into San Diego on Thursday evening after a 12-8 win in Colorado secured a series sweep that kept them in the wild-card hunt. They trail Philadelphia by two games and the Cubs by three.
“We came on this road trip knowing exactly what we needed to do and that’s win each day,” Arizona catcher James McCann said. “The focus and the talk in this clubhouse has been go 1-0 every day. That’s what we’ve done so far and that’s what we’re going to look to continue to do.
“We can’t control what other teams are doing, but we can control the way that we approach each and every day.”
Arizona has won its last five games to keep its hopes alive and will have one of its best pitchers, Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.72), starting the series opener. The right-hander last worked on Saturday night in his team’s 5-3 home win over the Yankees, allowing four hits and one run over 4 1/3 innings with a walk and three strikeouts.
Pfaadt is 2-0 in three outings this year against the Padres. He has won both of his starts, yielding one unearned run in 12 2/3 innings, and is 5-3 with a 3.82 ERA in 12 career appearances against them.
In his career, Pfaadt is 5-3 with an ERA of 3.82 and 12 starts in his career against San Diego. He has made one career start against
The teams have split their first 10 meetings this year, including a four-game series in San Diego from July 6-9.
–Field Level Media

item.title: [Field Level Media] Locked in as No. 2 seed, Dodgers turn to Tarik Skubal vs. Giants
item.description: Having seen their chances of gaining the top seed in the National League playoffs die in a two-game span, the Los Angeles Dodgers get an opportunity to coast into the postseason when they open a three-game road set against the San Francisco Giants on Friday. Left-hander Tarik Skubal (11-7, 2.85 ERA) is scheduled to get his final tune-up for the postseason in the series opener for the Dodgers. He will be opposed by Giants right-hander Yunior Marte (0-1, 4.66). While they can’t overtake the Milwau
item.content:encoded:
Having seen their chances of gaining the top seed in the National League playoffs die in a two-game span, the Los Angeles Dodgers get an opportunity to coast into the postseason when they open a three-game road set against the San Francisco Giants on Friday.
Left-hander Tarik Skubal (11-7, 2.85 ERA) is scheduled to get his final tune-up for the postseason in the series opener for the Dodgers. He will be opposed by Giants right-hander Yunior Marte (0-1, 4.66).
While they can’t overtake the Milwaukee Brewers for the best record, the Dodgers (97-62) have clinched the NL West title and the second-best record in the league. The latter will earn them a first-round bye in the playoffs, meaning after Sunday’s regular-season finale in San Francisco, they won’t play again until next Saturday.
Skubal will be making his 10th start since he was acquired from the Detroit Tigers at the trade deadline. Los Angeles has won seven of his nine outings, including the last six.
Skubal wasn’t particularly effective in a five-inning start against the Giants last Saturday in which he allowed four runs, two on a home run by Victor Bericoto. The Dodgers supported him with seven runs in those five innings, allowing him to walk away with a win.
He has faced the Giants just three times in his career, going 2-1 with a 4.30 ERA.
Skubal should have additional firepower supporting him in the rematch as the Dodgers have brought Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages back from injuries over the last three days.
Each got extensive playing time in the just-completed home series against the Padres, with Pages playing in all three games and Ohtani the last two, each going 3-for-9.
Both are expected to play significantly against the Giants, with the team getting five days off to start next week.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman said about the importance of the first-round bye. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here. It’s good to get those guys (Ohtani and Pages) back on the field, get some ABs in them and then rest up.”
Skubal will be matched up once again with Marte, who allowed six runs in 4 2/3 innings in the meeting in Los Angeles last week. A rookie facing the Dodgers for the first time, he served up a home run to Will Smith in taking the loss in his fourth major league appearance.
The Dodgers could see a familiar face late in the game with the Giants on Thursday having claimed their former closer, Camilo Doval, on waivers from the Pirates.
After 4 1/2 seasons in San Francisco in which he recorded 107 saves and was an All-Star in 2023, the Giants sent Doval to the New York Yankees last July for four prospects. One year and one day later, the Yankees flipped the right-hander to Pittsburgh, which in turn saw him pitch just 20 times before cutting him loose, allowing the Giants to snatch him back.
Interestingly, should Doval or another newcomer — catcher Zach Morgan — get into a game during the Dodgers series, the Giants (65-94) would tie the major-league record for number of players used in a season with 71. Should they both play, they would break the record.
Giants manager Tony Vitello joked to reporters Wednesday about the possibility of setting the record.
“I guess, you know, being the first year in the organization, you’d like to get to meet everybody,” he said. “So this is one way to do it.”
–Field Level Media

- In recent years, it's been extremely rare for a player who qualifies for the batting average title to go homerless in a season. Yet, the Rays' Chandler Simpson is on track to do just that, writes Davy Andrews at Fangraphs.

"The guy that used to hit .300, I'm sorry to tell you, is going to hit .240, .250 today. It just is what it is."@JoeyVotto breaks down why the league does not have more players like Luis Arraez and explains how baseball's evolution has led to that trend. pic.twitter.com/3C5fEUsv1s

item.content:encoded:
It should be a fun weekend in terms of which player wins the MLB home run crown, but I'll be happy either way because it will be either former Cub Kyle Schwarber or current Cubbies superstar and NL MVP lock Pete Crow-Armstrong as they are tied for the overall lead with 45 dingers apiece. I'd actually be fine with a tie. And both should play most of the weekend because their respective teams are playing for better NL wild card seeding. Not sure I see an advantage with both priced -110 to win it.
Those who want to get into , particularly home run prop betting, need to take a look at what I'm playing for Friday's games. Over the past four MLB seasons, I'm up $1,681 on MLB picks. You can find more of my picks at SportsLine, and in the member-exclusive SportsLine Discord server, a community of sports betting enthusiasts and SportsLine experts.
Last Friday, my home run picks were the Diamondbacks' Nolan Arenado at +630 vs. the Yankees as well as the Braves' Mike Yastrzemski +630 against the Astros. Arenado didn't homer but had two hits so I cashed Over 1.5 total bases -- all my home run prop picks mean I like Over 1.5 total bases even better at the . Yaz, meanwhile, was 0-for-4 with two strikeouts. Bummer.
Top MLB home run picks for Friday, Sept. 25
- Pete Alonso, Orioles (+394, DrafKings)
- Drake Baldwin, Braves (+360, FanDuel)
Pete Alonso, Orioles (+394, DraftKings)
This three-game AL East series between Baltimore and New York from Yankee Stadium that begins tonight at 7:05 ET is meaningless in the grand scheme of things. The Bombers are locked into the AL's top wild card spot and the Orioles are eliminated and can't even finish with a winning record. So long story short, I won't be betting a side here. WT.
I personally won't be touching any playoff-bound stars this weekend in terms of props because they might sit out or be pulled midway through a game to rest up and be as healthy as possible for the postseason, which starts Tuesday. And we've already been told by the Yankees that Aaron Judge will not be back from his latest injury for the Wild Card Series. That's a bummer. Although he claims he will play. We shall see.
But certainly there are players out there who have individual goals they want to meet by Sunday either for personal reasons or a financial incentive via bonus. Pete Alonso was Baltimore's big-ticket free-agent addition, and Alonso struggled early on as many stars do when leaving a team for the first time in free agency. But Alonso has been raking for weeks and could win the AL home run title. He currently has 41 and is in a four-way tie for first.
Alonso has become the first Orioles player since Anthony Santander in 2024 to get to 40 dingers, and Alonso already has easily cashed Over his spring total of 37.5. He was named the team MVP this week, the first unanimous Most Valuable Oriole since outfielder Cedric Mullins in 2021. While Alonso is a righty masher, he has a lot better numbers against right-handed pitchers and faces one tonight in New York's Will Warren (10-6, 4.02 ERA), who has given up 20 homers on the year. Alonso is 2-for-7 off him with two solo homers. I can't really recommend any other Orioles batters.
Drake Baldwin, Braves (+360, FanDuel)
An NL East series between Atlanta and Miami starts at 7:05 ET from South Florida, and I'm guessing there will be plenty of good seats available on a beautiful Florida fall night with high school football going strong. No weather concerns as the retractable roof at loanDepot Park is usually closed. They all are usually closed.
There is nothing at stake here, so I'm hoping the Braves include Drake Baldwin in the lineup. They are the NL East champions and will host the last NL wild card team in that round next week. I hope that's Philadelphia just for rivalry purposes. About the only carrot for the Marlins is to finish at .500.
If Miami can find some hitting in the offseason, it could be pretty decent in 2027 (if there is a season) because the Marlins have some good starting pitching led by fire-balling righty Eury Perez (7-11, 4.14 ERA), who goes tonight. Perez made his first career relief appearance on Tuesday at the Cubs in a 12-inning game but that will basically serve as his off-day bullpen session having thrown just one inning. Perez has surrendered 20 homers on the year.
With Seattle's Cal Raleigh falling way off this year, you could argue that lefty-hitting Drake Baldwin of the Braves is the best all-around offensive catcher in MLB -- although he plays at DH plenty. Baldwin has 24 homers and a slugging percentage of .456. Baldwin's power has disappeared a bit in September with only two homers, but he's 4-for-9 off Perez with two homers.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Braves' Ronald Acuna Jr. hopes to feast on Marlins
item.description: Ronald Acuna Jr. returned to action on Thursday and is expected to be in the lineup again on Friday night when his Atlanta Braves open a three-game series at the Miami Marlins to close the regular season. Sure, the Braves (93-66) already have clinched their seventh National League East title over the past nine years, but getting Acuna back up to speed is paramount. A five-time All-Star and the 2023 NL Most Valuable Player, Acuna went 2-for-5 on Thursday and scored a run in a 7-6 loss to the Cinc
item.content:encoded:
Ronald Acuna Jr. returned to action on Thursday and is expected to be in the lineup again on Friday night when his Atlanta Braves open a three-game series at the Miami Marlins to close the regular season.
Sure, the Braves (93-66) already have clinched their seventh National League East title over the past nine years, but getting Acuna back up to speed is paramount.
A five-time All-Star and the 2023 NL Most Valuable Player, Acuna went 2-for-5 on Thursday and scored a run in a 7-6 loss to the Cincinnati Reds. He missed Wednesday’s game vs. the Reds after suffering a bruised left shin on Tuesday in the series opener.
For the season, Acuna has an .813 OPS. This also is his first year with at least 20 homers and 20 steals since his MVP season.
“He’s a freakish athlete with crazy talent,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said of Acuna, 28. “He’s fun to watch when he’s like this.”
Weiss was referencing Acuna’s 1.119 OPS from Aug. 28 until his shin injury Tuesday, ranking him second in the majors in that category during that span.
“When (Acuna is) healthy and on one of these streaks, he’s one of the best players in baseball,” Braves second baseman Ozzie Albies told MLB.com.
Acuna leads the Braves with 21 steals — 52 fewer than he had in 2023. Acuna’s 20 homers this season ranks fifth on the team behind first baseman Matt Olson (41), center fielder Michael Harris II (26), catcher Drake Baldwin (24) and Albies (22).
The Braves, who have not announced their starter for Friday’s game, will face Marlins right-hander Eury Perez (7-11, 4.14 ERA).
Perez has never beaten the Braves, going 0-3 with a 9.78 ERA in five starts.
This will be Perez’s last start of 2026, and he is in dire need of a good performance. After posting an ERA under 1.85 in seven starts in June and July, Perez slipped a bit in August (3.46). Then, in five appearances in September, he has an 8.84 ERA.
As a team, the Marlins (78-81) need to sweep the Braves to avoid their third straight losing season. Miami needs two wins to improve on last season’s 79-win campaign.
Unfortunately for the Marlins, closer Pete Fairbanks (team-high 19 saves) is on the injured list. The remaining bullpen leaders are Calvin Faucher (3.34 ERA in 68 games), Michael Petersen (3.08 in 64), Tyler Zuber (5.67 in 44) and Josh Ekness (3.34 in 29).
Earlier this week, Ekness hit 102 mph on the radar gun. It was the second-fastest pitch thrown by a Marlins player since that data started to be recorded in 2008. Only Tyron Guerrero (102.5 mph in 2018) has thrown harder.
“I didn’t know I was capable of throwing a ball that hard,” Ekness told mlb.com.
As for Miami’s offense, shortstop Otto Lopez — a first-time All-Star this year — is on the verge of finishing his season hitting .300 or above. That would be another first-time feat for Lopez, who currently is batting .304.
–Field Level Media

item.title: [MLB.com] 5 things to define the Orioles' last three games of 2026
item.dc:creator: Jake Rill
item.description: NEW YORK -- The Orioles will not be heading to the 2026 postseason. Although the O’s were off on Thursday, they were eliminated from playoff contention when the White Sox recorded a 9-1 win at Kansas City and clinched a berth for themselves. Baltimore’s odds of reaching the postseason had been low for quite some time. With only three games remaining on the schedule (all vs. the Yankees in New York this weekend), the Orioles will look to finish strong and build positive momentum toward the offsea
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- The Orioles will not be heading to the 2026 postseason.
Although the O’s were off on Thursday, they were eliminated from playoff contention when the White Sox recorded a 9-1 win at Kansas City and clinched a berth for themselves. Baltimore’s odds of reaching the postseason had been low for quite some time.
With only three games remaining on the schedule (all vs. the Yankees in New York this weekend), the Orioles will look to finish strong and build positive momentum toward the offseason. And while no playoff stakes will be involved, there are still things to watch for.
Here are five things to keep an eye on during Baltimore’s final series of the season.
With only three games remaining on the schedule (all vs. the Yankees in New York this weekend), the Orioles will look to finish strong and build positive momentum toward the offseason. And while no playoff stakes will be involved, there are still things to watch for.
Here are five things to keep an eye on during Baltimore’s final series of the season.
1. Attempting to finish .500
The O’s can’t end up with a winning record, but they can still get to .500. However, they’ll need to sweep the three-game set at Yankee Stadium to make that happen, and they haven’t swept a series of three-plus games in the Bronx since June 6-8, 1986.
Baltimore is guaranteed to have a better record than it did in 2025 (75-87). It hasn’t had a year in which it finished exactly .500 since going 81-81 in 2015.
“Regardless of what the record is, I just want to play good baseball, good quality baseball, and whatever we have left in the tank, just empty the tank. Because after 162, that's it, you’ve got to wait until spring,” first baseman Pete Alonso said. “Hopefully, we win all three, because that's the goal. We want to win every game that we play, regardless of the standings.”
2. How many more homers can Alonso hit?
Through 159 games, Alonso has clubbed a team-high 41 home runs during his first season with the Orioles. And he’ll surely play all three at Yankee Stadium, as he hasn’t missed a game since the 2023 season.
Here’s the list of 41-plus-homer seasons in O’s history (since 1954):
1. Chris Davis -- 53 in 2013
2. Brady Anderson -- 50 in 1996
3. Frank Robinson -- 49 in 1966
T-4. Davis -- 47 in 2015
T-4. Mark Trumbo -- 47 in 2016
6. Jim Gentile -- 46 in 1961
7. Anthony Santander -- 44 in 2024
8. Rafael Palmeiro -- 43 in 1998
9. Alonso -- 41 in 2026
Considering Alonso has six home runs over his past eight games (including three during a three-game sweep of Toronto earlier this week), it’s possible the 31-year-old slugger will add a few more to his total, potentially passing Palmeiro and perhaps even Santander.
3. RBI history for Alonso?
Another feat that Alonso could accomplish is one no player has done before.
There’s never been an MLB player to post a pair of seasons in which he led each of the two leagues (American and National) in RBIs, since RBIs became official in 1920. Alonso led the NL with 131 RBIs in 2022, and this year, he leads the AL with 110.
4. More of The Mountain
Félix Bautista made an emotional return to the Orioles earlier this week after missing more than a year due to right shoulder surgery. The 31-year-old former All-Star closer was quite familiar with long recoveries, as he previously missed all of the 2024 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery.
Bautista has made a pair of appearances since rejoining Baltimore’s bullpen. He allowed one run in two-thirds of an inning vs. the Brewers on Sunday, then yielded two runs in one inning against the Blue Jays on Wednesday.
The results aren’t too important at the moment, especially because Bautista hasn’t yet reassumed his closing duties. But it’s encouraging that he’s getting a few big league outings in before entering the offseason and looking to return to his previously dominant form in 2027.
“I stayed firm the entire time, focused on the hard work,” Bautista recently said via team interpreter Brandon Quinones. “I knew that it was just as long of a road [as Tommy John], and it took a lot of time. But my entire focus the entire time was just on the work itself.”
5. Trevor Rogers’ potential final O’s start
The winner of the 2025 Most Valuable Oriole Award, Rogers has been one of Baltimore’s best starters over the past two seasons. The 28-year-old left-hander has a 4.07 ERA in 29 starts, but he had some struggles early in the year. Since June 4, he has a 2.92 ERA over 19 starts.
Rogers is scheduled to start Game 2 of Friday’s doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. Will it be his final time pitching for the Orioles? He is set to become a free agent after the season, but it’s possible he’ll re-sign with the club. (He could also be a prime candidate to receive a qualifying offer, which would bring him back for one more year.)

item.title: [Yardbarker] Juan Soto assigns blame for disastrous Mets season
item.dc:creator: Zac Wassink
item.description: What became a disastrous season for the New York Mets will mercifully come to an end this coming Sunday afternoon. While speaking with Mike Puma of the New York Post following the Mets' 3-1 loss at the Texas Rangers on Thursday, star outfielder Juan Soto pointed a finger at himself for the current state of the club. "It’s definitely not what I imagined in my head," Soto said about the Mets' campaign, per Phillip Martinez of SNY. "There is nothing I can do other than blame myself. I have got to b
item.content:encoded:
What became a disastrous season for the New York Mets will mercifully come to an end this coming Sunday afternoon.
While speaking with Mike Puma of the New York Post following the Mets' 3-1 loss at the Texas Rangers on Thursday, star outfielder Juan Soto pointed a finger at himself for the current state of the club.
"It’s definitely not what I imagined in my head," Soto said about the Mets' campaign, per Phillip Martinez of SNY. "There is nothing I can do other than blame myself. I have got to be better. I have got to be at the level to take us forward."
Soto and shortstop Francisco Lindor were supposed to help carry the Mets after team president of baseball operations David Stearns controversially dismantled the core of the club's roster last offseason. Instead, separate calf injuries limited Soto to just 108 games through Thursday afternoon. Over those contests, he slashed .274/.393/.522 with an OPS of .915, 27 home runs and 68 RBI.
That said, Soto is optimistic about the future of a team that features young talents such as Carson Benge, fellow outfielder A.J. Ewing, potential ace Nolan McLean, starting pitcher Christian Scott and others.
"We have a young core, and we have got to maintain that young core and encourage them to the right way, the right path for the future," Soto explained. "I think we are going in the right direction. Look at the young core and what they have been doing their first year in the big leagues. I think it’s real special. It’s always the first and second years are probably the toughest ones of your career, so what they’re doing, I think, is very special."
One can only guess what MLB will look like whenever the expected work stoppage comes to an end, and it's unclear how uncertainty related to the state of the league will impact what clubs do this coming fall. Soto made it clear that he wants Stearns and big-spending Mets owner Steve Cohen to be aggressive in an attempt to engineer a quick turnaround for the franchise.
"We should go and get as much as we can," Soto added. "We need as much help as we can get. It was a real tough year for us, so I think we have got to go out there and grab as much as we can."
The 73-86 Mets will begin a season-closing three-game series at the rival Washington Nationals (75-84) on Friday evening.

Guerrero seemed to express remorse about his disappointing season, but his remarks weren’t perceive
item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s not wrong, but he’s also not right
Photo credit: Cary Edmondson-Imagn Images
The Toronto Blue Jays’ offseason hasn’t even begun, but the club is already the talk of baseball thanks to the face of their franchise, Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
He may have put his foot in his mouth when his comments made the rounds earlier this week after an interview with podcaster Veronica Batista. Guerrero seemed to express remorse about his disappointing season, but his remarks weren’t perceived that way by some fans.
First of all, the timing of this interview could not have been worse. The video came out the day the Blue Jays were eliminated from postseason contention. It’s almost as if it were planned that way for maximum exposure and general outrage.
Had this interview taken place earlier this season, or during the offseason, there would be a different tenor about it. But with a lot of vitriol among the Blue Jays fan base, these comments have not sat well among Jays devotees.
There are some areas where he’s right and some areas where he’s wrong. The comment that drew the most ire was Guerrero saying, “They didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished.”
Is this Vladdy saying the quiet part out loud, or is there credence to what he said?
Professional baseball players are criminally underpaid at the beginning of their careers. To earn the league minimum through the first three years of their Major League journey, followed by three years of arbitration (four if you’re lucky to reach Super Two status), is a big reason many teams can afford to keep their productive players.
The value that Guerrero provided at the beginning of his career far exceeded what he was paid before he signed his monster contract. According to FanGraphs’ Value metric, Vladdy provided $164 million in value through his first seven seasons in the big leagues while earning $72.5 million.
Anyone aside from MLB owners would agree the salary arbitration model is broken, so it’s easy to see why Guerrero feels like his $500 million contract is a delayed payment for his early-career production. Surely, there are many MLB players who are silently yelling “PREACH” after hearing what Guerrero said.
In that moment, Vlad was acting as an advocate for his fellow players. Given that the players and owners are hurtling toward a lockout on December 2, his stance was understandable. He is one of the faces of Major League Baseball, so as Vlad goes, so too does the rest of the league.
But that’s not how modern-day contracts work. Nine-figure deals paying for past production may be a Pollyanna perspective held by some professional athletes, but those contracts bank on future production more than the past. As much as MLB executives might spin it to the players as a thank you for services tendered, it’s not totally accurate.
Guerrero should be given some grace, as not everything he said in the video (and the follow-up comments) was flame-worthy. In a way, he admitted the pressure of the $500 million contract is weighing on him, which is to be expected for any 27-year-old handed the keys to the Blue Jays for the next 13 years.
Although Guerrero surely meant no harm during that interview, he had to have known his comments would be unnerving to folks in Toronto. The optics are bad, and this is a PR blunder. At the very least, his handlers should’ve had a better grasp on the temperature of the Blue Jays fan base and asked to delay the release of the interview, rather than have it drop at the worst possible moment.
After the disappointing season Vlad had, some fans wanted their pound of flesh, and anything less than a full admission of ineptitude wouldn’t suffice. When a player carries a team like Guerrero did in the postseason last year and then virtually disappears the following season, people want answers.
Vlad didn’t have an answer that made anyone feel better about how 2026 went down, which may be the underlying reason for all this venom in the first place. Guerrero can’t just “aw shucks” a single-digit home run total and sub-.700 OPS season away, but for baseball players, compartmentalizing failure is what makes them successful.
Had Vladdy missed significant time this season due to injuries, there would be a little more tolerance for his underperformance. The fact that he played 140+ games this year, claiming to not be injured, almost makes it worse because his regression can’t be blamed on an injury.
I don’t believe the Blue Jays have buyer’s remorse already, but this is the risk you run plunking a half-billion dollars into one player. If they carry the team on their back, they’re the GOAT. If they fail, they’re the goat.
It’s an apples-to-oranges situation, but the Boston Red Sox ran Rafael Devers out of town after giving him the keys to Beantown. A few years after inking a 10-year, $331 million extension, the fracture between Devers and the Red Sox front office grew so wide that he was traded to the San Francisco Giants.
I’m not saying the same fate befalls Toronto’s golden child, but we’re already starting to witness the side effects of tying up so much money in one player. The fan base hasn’t turned on Guerrero, but this could start to get ugly if he fails to turn things around in 2027.
2026 will not only be remembered as a golden opportunity missed by the Blue Jays but also by Vladdy himself. Guerrero wasn’t wrong with many of the things he said, but he also wasn’t right. The timing was atrocious, but hey, isn’t that typical of Toronto sports?

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yordan Alvarez Takes Historic Season to Level Never Seen Before by Astros
item.dc:creator: Yirsandy Rodriguez; Unknown
item.description: Yordan Alvarez’s great season with the Houston Astros is also generating headlines beyond his pursuit of the Triple Crown and his MVP case. After going 2-for-4 in the Astros’ 6-5 loss to the Seattle Mariners on Wednesday, Alvarez led MLB in batting average (.314), on-base percentage (.431) and slugging percentage (.601). item.content:encoded:
Yordan Alvarez’s great season with the Houston Astros is also generating headlines beyond his pursuit of the Triple Crown and his MVP case.
After going 2-for-4 in the Astros’ 6-5 loss to the Seattle Mariners on Wednesday, Alvarez led MLB in batting average (.314), on-base percentage (.431) and slugging percentage (.601).
The last three players to lead the Major Leagues in all three offensive percentage categories were Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (2025), and the now-retired Miguel Cabrera (2013) and Barry Bonds (2002).
The run scored by Alvarez in the third inning was the 100th of the season, to which he added 106 walks and 102 RBIs. These numbers put his season on another level, as only Judge and Bonds have been able to add at least 100 walks and 100 runs scored to their season while leading the offensive line. Entering his final three games against the Athletics, he can add to that.
Judge did it in 2025 when he led the league with 124 walks and 137 runs scored, while Bonds completed those numbers in 2002 and then again in 2004 when he walked 232 times.
An Unmatched Season in Astros History
Alvarez's season has been historic. In addition to leading the offense, he has added triple digits in runs scored, RBIs and walks, which puts his 2026 season in a historic place. No other Houston hitter has been able to achieve those three marks in a single season and, at the same time, lead the Majors in batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage.
Jeff Bagwell is the one who came closest when he led the league with 143 runs scored and 149 walks in 1999 and accumulated 42 home runs with 126 RBIs, but his .304/.454/.591 offensive line could not lead the Majors. Bagwell also had great seasons as an Astro in 1997 and 2000 without being able to reach Alvarez's impact, and something similar happened with Lance Berkman in 2002 (he led the league with 128 RBIs, scored 106 runs and took 107 walks) and Alex Bregman in 2019 (he led the league with 119 walks, drove in 112 and scored 122 runs).
Alvarez is eight RBIs away from tying Pete Alonso, who leads the American League with 110, and that could make the big difference in the race to win the Triple Crown. However, he still remains in the conversation as a solid candidate for the American League MVP award. Since Carl Yastrzemski won the American League Triple Crown in 1967, Miguel Cabrera in 2012 has been the only Triple Crown winner in the Major Leagues.
In any case, the season is not over yet and there can be excitement in these final days. That said, he will have to unleash his swing as he did throughout the season, especially before August. In that same stretch since August 1, Alonso made the difference with 18 home runs, while Alvarez has been able to hit only six.
Houston continues its four-game series against the Athletics, which could be a great opportunity for him to drive the team and continue adding historic chapters to his great season.
Yirsandy is a baseball writer specializing in MLB coverage with experience across multiple teams and storylines. He currently writes for Diamond Centric, where he covers the New York Mets, San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, and Kansas City Royals. My work focuses on game coverage, player analysis, and storytelling that connects performance with context. My Substack has also been an important part of my writing development, where I’ve built much of my baseball coverage and storytelling voice over time. I’m passionate about combining reporting, research, and thoughtful analysis to produce engaging baseball content for readers.
Follow Yirsandy

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] 'It's emotional to think about': George Springer faces end of Blue Jays deal
item.dc:creator: Shi Davidi
item.description: TORONTO – Baseball is full of long days and short years, which is how it can simultaneously feel like George Springer’s been with the Toronto Blue Jays forever and that the six seasons in his then-club-record $150-million free-agent contract have flown by. item.content:encoded:
TORONTO – Baseball is full of long days and short years, which is how it can simultaneously feel like George Springer’s been with the Toronto Blue Jays forever and that the six seasons in his then-club-record $150-million free-agent contract have flown by.
So much has happened since he signed that fateful agreement Jan. 23, 2021, while the federal government’s pandemic restrictions that locked the club out of its home for a season-and-a-half were still in place.
Despite 91 wins, the Blue Jays missed the playoffs by one measly game in that vagabond three-home-sites ’21 season, before jarring wild-card exits followed in each of the next two years.
As a three-stage renovation completely transformed the Rogers Centre, a train-wreck 2024 was chased by the exhilarating run to — and subsequent heartbreak of — the 2025 World Series, the slugger delivering a franchise-pantheon Game 7 ALCS homer along the way.
He earned an all-star selection and a Silver Slugger, poured into his teammates, set a standard in the clubhouse, became a symbol of the club’s re-emergence as a legitimate player in the free-agent market and is so ingrained within the organization’s fabric that his seven preceding seasons with the Houston Astros feel more like fever dream than reality.
Yet suddenly, the end is nigh, with three games versus the visiting Cincinnati Reds beginning Friday night (7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT, Sportsnet, Sportsnet+) all that remains of those six years, and perhaps in his career, too.
“It’s emotional to think about it,” Springer said Wednesday in a quiet corner of the visitors' clubhouse at Camden Yards, after an Orioles doubleheader sweep eliminated the Blue Jays from the wild-card chase. “Very, very grateful to our fans, this team, this organization. Obviously this is not the way that we all wanted it to end. But if it is, I'm going to do my best to embrace being back home for one last time and making sure that I do anything I can to reciprocate to the fans.”
Springer is coy about the future beyond that, although some close to him expect that he will retire once all is said and done. At 37, having willed his way through far more ailments than he will acknowledge, having won one World Series, tainted as it may be by the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal, and come within inches of another, with 308 homers and a career OPS of .823 over 13 seasons, his resume is substantial.
His final season — .251/.323/.407 with 15 homers and 54 RBIs — would surely look different if a foul tip hadn’t fractured his left big toe May 11 and forced him to play compromised for weeks once he returned.
In 58 games since the all-star break, though, he’s posted an .800 OPS with six homers and 32 RBIs, demonstrating that even through subsequent shoulder issues, he can still do damage. Combined with his veteran leadership and experience, there is sure to be a market for him during the off-season, if he wants to continue playing.
Does he?
“I don't know,” he replied. “I love this organization. I loved being a Blue Jay. I've loved every single bit of being here. I haven't really gotten that far yet. I've kind of taken every day with these guys in stride.”
As he usually does, Springer shrugged off the toll his aggressive style has taken on him physically and insisted that won’t tip the scales in his decision-making.
“If my mind can say it, then my body can do it – my body can do whatever I tell it to do, hopefully,” he said. “But I'll cross that road once I get to it. We've still got to get through these next three and then we'll go into the off-season and I'll see what happens.”
More of a factor will be the needs of his family as Springer and wife Charlise have three sons aged five, three and three-months-old. The two older boys have been clubhouse staples this season, often walking around with either a bat or a glove in hand, following their dad through each stage of his pre-game. During a recent homestand, they each took a round of batting practice on the field once the Blue Jays were done and ran the bases after.
“It's hard to be away from them and to miss things,” said Springer. “I want to be able to give them hugs and say, I love you in person. It's been a long year for me off the field. But those are my kids and I love them. I'll sit down with my wife at the end of this year and we'll discuss whatever's going to happen. But I love my family and if that requires me to be with them, I'll be with them.”
In some ways that would be a natural transition, given the way Springer’s grown into a father-figure type during his time with the Blue Jays.
During one down stretch in May, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. pointed out that “George is my advice guy,” and praised Springer for telling him to “go out there and be yourself, laughing, joking” because “sometimes you put too much pressure and then sometimes you change your body language, so he always tells us to go out there and have fun.”
Myles Straw, who also played with Springer in Houston, recently praised the way he brought calmness and energy through games of increasing leverage, saying, “I've seen George do it for years now … Even in the playoffs, it's like Game 1 of the season for George.”
Manager John Schneider, who’s praised Springer in so many ways over the years, pointed out last month how important his guidance was through this summer’s trade deadline, when the Blue Jays traded away Kevin Gausman, Daulton Varsho and Jeff Hoffman but still crawled back into contention.
“That's part of the reason we signed him when we did, he's remarkably aware of how things can change and he doesn't panic,” said Schneider. “That rubs off on everyone and his will to say like, ‘Hey, I'm going to do whatever it takes to win today,’ has rubbed off on some guys. He's been great. He's still having fun and he's still affecting people around him.”
During his 3.5 seasons with the Blue Jays, Varsho grew especially close to Springer, who’d regularly walk through the clubhouse calling, “Daulton,” when he couldn’t find the centre-fielder.
“I’m going to cherish every moment that we've had together because he's taught me a lot about myself, just what it means to be a leader and how to do it in the right way,” Varsho said Aug. 1. “He's a lead-by-example guy and he'll use his voice every once in a while when he needs to. It's a pretty spectacular career he's had. Obviously I keep talking to him, I want him to keep playing, but obviously for him it's his choice and his family's choice. But he's had a hell of a career and it's always been enjoyable for me to play alongside him.”
All combined, it’s a sizable legacy Springer has carved out with the Blue Jays, who signed him to push the franchise to the next level and saw him do precisely that. At the time of his 2021 signing, president and CEO Mark Shapiro said, “there's no limit to what this market can be, it's a behemoth and we're going to continue to get better and continue to add the players and keep the players that we have necessary to be a championship team year-in, year-out.”
In that way, the Blue Jays achieved what they envisioned — save for the championship — when they invested in Springer six years ago.
Asked if he’s accomplished all he wanted with Toronto, minus the title, Springer replied, “I don't know. I hope so.”
“I’d hope that over the last six years, I've been able to show the fans and this organization that I love them and I'll play as hard as I can every single day with whatever I've got,” he continued. “At the end of the day, the goal was to win the World Series and we came an eyelash shy. But to see all the progress that we made as organization and a team, just to be standing on that field in Game 7 was a dream come true for me. So yeah, I'd love to be the last team standing, but this has been a hell of a six years.”
One series left. Time sure does fly.

item.title: [heavy.com] Astros Legend George Springer Shares Retirement Feelings
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Even though George Springer no longer plays for the Houston Astros, he’ll always be regarded as one of the best to ever put on the franchise’s uniform. And now with the Toronto Blue Jays, Springer has entered the part of his MLB career where it’s time to at least start wondering about retirement.
