item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO — Before the regular season concludes on Sunday, manager Tony Vitello has one last piece of business to address.
The Giants have already used 70 different players this season, surpassing the previous franchise record (66) set under former president of baseball operations Farhan Zaidi. With three games remaining, a weekend homestand against the Dodgers that begins Friday night, Vitello has one more player who needs to see the field before it’s all said and done.
Zach Morgan, who grew up in Stockton as a Giants fan, spent eight games on San Francisco’s roster this season but has yet to debut. The 26-year-old catcher rejoined the team on the taxi squad on Wednesday after Osleivis Basabe’s hamstring flared up the previous day. Vitello said he is going to find a way to get him into a game.
“Come hell or high water, I’d like to get him on that field and give him an opportunity to do something,” Vitello said.
If and when Morgan makes his major-league debut, the Giants will tie the 2025 Atlanta Braves for the most players used in a single season. When Vitello was asked about using so many players before Wednesday’s 4-2 loss to the Minnesota Twins, the first-year manager at least had a sense of humor.
“I guess being first year in the organization, you’d like to get to meet everybody,” Vitello said. “So, this is one way to do it.”
Given the amount of established regulars on the Opening Day roster, the Giants could never have envisioned needing so many players to get through one of the worst and weirdest seasons in franchise history. It’s a dizzying roster churn that’s largely been the product of an absolutely ruthless injury bug.
Since last Friday, San Francisco has placed four players — Logan Webb, Bryce Eldridge, Jung Hoo Lee and Blade Tidwell — on the injured list. Eldridge landed in concussion protocol after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles last week, while Lee sustained a groin contusion after fouling a ball off a sensitive area.
As for Tidwell, he’s likely headed for surgery after being diagnosed with a “high-grade” UCL sprain and could miss the entire 2027 season. Tidwell will become the Giants’ fourth young starter to undergo a UCL procedure this year, joining Hayden Birdsong, Trevor McDonald and Carson Whisenhunt.
Since August, Casey Schmitt (torn meniscus), Matt Chapman (core), Rafael Devers (core) and Daniel Susac (patella fracture) have undergone season-ending surgery. Willy Adames didn’t go under the knife, but the left elbow sprain he sustained in late August ended up ending his season.
There’s also Harrison Bader, who played just 30 games after sustaining multiple injuries, then crashing into a fire truck while riding a scooter in the wee hours of the morning.
The Giants currently have 16 players on the 60-day injured list, and according to FanGraphs’ Jon Becker, the last team with that many players on their 60-day IL was the 2021 Texas Rangers. San Francisco’s brass will have many cuts to make in the offseason, especially with prospects such as Henry Lalane and Marty Gair eligible for the Rule 5 Draft (which may not happen due to the impending lockout).
Among those on the Opening Day roster, only infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp remain, the latter of whom was shut down for the rest of the season.
“Odd is a good word,” Koss said. “I would have to look up how many times it’s happened in a baseball season. I imagine it’s pretty low. It’s kind of one of those things we’ve had to deal with this season.”
Injuries aren’t the only reason why the Giants have called on so many different names.
Seven members of the Opening Day roster – Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez, Robbie Ray, Erik Miller, Tyler Mahle, Caleb Kilian — were shipped to other teams this season. Bailey was shockingly traded to the Cleveland Guardians in May, but the rest of the bunch was dealt right before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
The abnormal roster churn has led to its share of odd facts and figures.
San Francisco has also had a franchise-record 17 players make their MLB debuts, the latest being outfielder Bo Davidson. Vitello has also used 15 different leadoff hitters, tied for the most used by a single team in MLB history (since at least 1898).
The Giants have had six different players homer while playing catcher this season which, per Sarah Langs, is tied with the 2022 Reds and 2019 A’s for the most in a single season. Five players — César Perdomo (No. 83), Seth Lonsway (No. 86), Braxton Roxby (No. 90), Scott Bandura (No. 91) and Davidson (No. 94) — have worn numbers that have never previously been used in franchise history.
For Vitello, if there is any semblance of a silver lining, it’s that he’s experienced “so many cool moments and be a part of kids’ lives.” On Wednesday, Vitello recalled seeing video of Davidson’s family celebrate his first career hit, a single to cap off a nine-pitch at-bat.
“That’s been a huge bright spot on a year where there’s been a lot of days — full transparency — back in the locker room that aren’t too pretty,” Vitello said.

item.content:encoded:
Sep 24, 2026, 11:58 AM ET
Across 182 innings (31 starts) in 2026, Seattle Mariners starting pitcher Logan Gilbert has recorded a 12-11 record with a 3.81 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 197 strikeouts. While Gilbert has still been a very useful pitcher for fantasy managers, he hasn't been quite as dominant this season as he has been in his peak years. After posting a 32.3% strikeout rate in 2025, Gilbert's strikeout rate has fallen to 26.7% in 2026. The 29-year-old's numbers have taken a considerable hit lately, as he's posted a 6.65 ERA across 21 2/3 innings in September. Surrendering the long ball has been a major issue for Gilbert in the second half of the season. Across 56 1/3 innings (10 starts) since the beginning of August, Gilbert has allowed 14 home runs (2.20 HR/9). Heading into his final scheduled start of 2026 against the Los Angeles Angels on Sunday, fantasy managers may want to temper expectations for the usually dependable Gilbert.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
More Recent News
Sep 24, 2026, 11:47 AM ET
Across 653 plate appearances in 2026, San Diego Padres outfielder Jackson Merrill is hitting .252/.300/.459 with 26 home runs, 86 RBI, 82 runs scored, and 26 stolen bases. The 23-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, hitting .219 with 10 home runs across 396 plate appearances before the All-Star break. However, Merrill has been red hot in the second half, hitting .300 with 16 homers across his last 261 trips to the plate. Merrill has been particularly key to San Diego's late-season surge as an offense, hitting .325 with four home runs, 16 RBI, 10 runs scored, and two stolen bases over his first 85 plate appearances in September. The star center fielder has lowered his strikeout rate this month to 18.8% while also posting elite barrel (19.7%) and hard-hit (62.1%) rates. Heading into San Diego's final weekend of the regular season, Merrill profiles as one of the top five-category producers in all of fantasy baseball.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:33 AM ET
Across 102 innings (19 starts) in 2026, Houston Astros right-hander Hunter Brown has recorded a 6-3 record with a 3.26 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 120 strikeouts. The 28-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, missing over two months with a shoulder injury and posting a 4.94 ERA across 27 1/3 innings in July. However, Brown has begun to rediscover his top form in recent outings. Across his last 33 1/3 innings (six starts), Brown is 3-0 with a 2.43 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, and 48 strikeouts. Brown has had issues with command all year long, and his 11.9% walk rate has led to an elevated WHIP. However, he's boosted his strikeout rate all the way up to 28.1% and has struck out 39.1% of the batters he's faced across his first four starts of September. Heading into his final start of the regular season on Saturday against the Athletics, Brown is beginning to look like the fantasy ace he was drafted to be ahead of 2026.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Across 501 plate appearances in 2026, Cleveland Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana is hitting .245/.337/.404 with 15 home runs, 57 RBI, 53 runs scored, and 19 stolen bases. The 24-year-old's underlying batted-ball metrics are underwhelming, as he's logged just a 4.8% barrel rate and a 36.2% hard-hit rate. However, Bazzana's 11.2% walk rate is impressive for a young player and helps him get on base consistently and use his speed. Bazzana has also been red-hot of late, hitting .288 with six home runs, 15 RBI, and 11 runs scored across 69 plate appearances in September. If the former top prospect is starting to grow into his power, he could begin to emerge as one of the better second base options for fantasy managers. In leagues where he's on the waiver wire, Bazzana should be a priority target for fantasy managers.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Across 655 plate appearances in 2026, Minnesota Twins first baseman Josh Bell is hitting .255/.317/.416 with 20 home runs, 92 RBI, 76 runs scored, and two stolen bases. The 34-year-old may not have one clear standout skill, but he remains a steady source of power and run production. Bell has kept his strikeout rate manageable at 19.9% while still posting solid barrel (9.5%) and hard-hit (42.0%) rates. The veteran switch-hitter also remains locked into everyday playing time in the heart of the Twins lineup, putting him in a good position to rack up runs and RBI. Heading into the final weekend of the regular season, Bell profiles as a balanced producer for fantasy managers to target on the waiver wire.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:10 AM ET
Across 444 plate appearances in 2026, Baltimore Orioles third baseman/first baseman Coby Mayo is hitting .225/.293/.463 with 24 home runs, 63 RBI, 63 runs scored, and four stolen bases. Swing-and-miss is the obvious red flag in Mayo's profile, as he's struck out in 30.2% of his plate appearances. However, the 24-year-old brings significant power upside with a 13.7% barrel rate and a 47.6% hard-hit rate. Mayo has hit .265 with 12 home runs since the All-Star break, and he's established himself as an everyday presence in the heart of the Baltimore lineup. For fantasy managers in need of power, Mayo profiles as a priority target on the waiver wire heading into the final weekend of the regular season.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Carlos Lagrange Could Join Yankees' Playoff Roster


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 12:02 AM ET
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that right-handed pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange is "in the conversation" for a spot on the team's postseason roster for the wild-card series next week against the division-rival Boston Red Sox, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. The 23-year-old Dominican is the team's No. 3 prospect at MLB Pipeline, and he has been ramping up his throwing program since coming off the seven-day injured list on Sept. 16 with a sprained right shoulder. Lagrange went 1-4 this year at Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, recording a 4.48 ERA, 1.35 WHIP, and 85:33 K:BB in 64 1/3 innings pitched across 19 appearances (11 starts). If Lagrange is pulled up to the Yankees' playoff roster, he would be making his major-league debut in the postseason in a relief role out of the bullpen. The 6-foot-7, 248-pounder has the tools to excel in high-leverage spots with an upper-90s fastball with armside run and multiple secondary pitches that can generate swings and misses consistently.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
Sep 23, 2026, 11:52 PM ET
Chicago Cubs right-hander Kevin Gausman (shoulder) came up wincing and in some apparent pain after diving to tag a runner out at third base during his start on Wednesday at Wrigley Field against the visiting Miami Marlins, according to Tony Andracki. Gausman was pulled from the game, but he was also at 101 pitches on the night. Manager Craig Counsell said that Gausman's left shoulder got extended awkwardly and "grabbed on him" on the play. He is now sore, and the Cubs will see how he feels in the next couple of days. Gausman is lined up to potentially start Game 1 or 2 next week in the wild-card series in the playoffs. The good news for the Cubs is that the injury is to the veteran's non-throwing arm as well. He came one out shy of a quality start for his fantasy managers on Wednesday, allowing two earned runs on six hits (one homer) while walking one and striking out seven in 5 2/3 frames for a no-decision. The 35-year-old veteran came into his final start of the regular season with a 9-12 record, 4.55 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 177 strikeouts in 172 innings pitched in 2026 with the Cubs and Toronto Blue Jays.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Tony Andracki
Sep 23, 2026, 10:59 PM ET
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that shortstop/second baseman Anthony Volpe could see some playing time at third base this week, per the Talkin' Yanks podcast. Volpe has mostly played shortstop in his MLB career, but he recently filled in at second base while Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. was sidelined by a thumb injury. With Chisholm Jr. back, it appears that New York could work Volpe into the mix at third base. The Yankees have gotten underwhelming production at the hot corner from Ryan McMahon, who has hit .210 with 11 home runs across 356 plate appearances in 2026. Volpe's numbers don't appear much better on the surface, as he's hit .244/.321/.335 with two home runs, 26 RBI, 24 runs scored, and 11 stolen bases across 234 plate appearances. However, the 25-year-old has been better in September, hitting .263 with four stolen bases across 40 trips to the plate this month.--Will Brady
Source: Talkin' Yanks
Chase Burns Working on Adding a Sinker


Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:47 PM ET
Cincinnati Reds starting pitcher Chase Burns (groin) was working on a sinker in his final starts before being placed on the 15-day injured list with a groin strain, per Charlie Goldsmith of the Charlie's Chalkboard Substack. Burns put together a dominant season in 2026, recording a 15-3 record with a 2.86 ERA, 1.17 WHIP, and 185 strikeouts across 154 1/3 innings (29 starts). However, Burns threw almost exclusively four-seam fastballs and sliders, mixing in the occasional changeup as well. Burns told Goldsmith that adding the sinker and continuing to develop his changeup should help him go deeper into games. If Burns can successfully add a sinker to his repertoire over the offseason, he could take his production to an even higher level in 2027.--Will Brady
Source: Charlie's Chalkboard - Charlie Goldsmith
Garrett Crochet Will Not Pitch this Week


Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:36 PM ET
Boston Red Sox left-hander Garrett Crochet (shoulder) will not appear in a regular-season game this week but is still in play to return during the postseason, per Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Crochet is currently on the 60-day injured list and has not pitched since late April due to shoulder and lat issues. However, he's been working toward a return and could be a factor out of the bullpen for Boston at some point in the playoffs. While 2026 has been a lost year for the 27-year-old, Crochet was one of the best pitchers in baseball in 2025. Across 205 1/3 innings (32 starts), he recorded an 18-5 record with a 2.59 ERA, 1.03 WHIP, and 255 strikeouts. Crochet also has experience as a reliever, making 54 appearances out of the bullpen for the Chicago White Sox in 2021.--Will Brady
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Sep 23, 2026, 10:27 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies starting pitcher Jesus Luzardo (shoulder) played catch for a fourth straight day on Wednesday and is expected to progress to mound work "very soon," per Matt Gelb of The Athletic. Luzardo has been sidelined since early September by shoulder inflammation, but it appears he has a chance to work out of the bullpen for the Phillies in the National League Wild Card Series. Across 178 2/3 innings (29 starts) before the injury, the 28-year-old recorded a 14-5 record with a 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, and 221 strikeouts. Luzardo posted a career-best 30.4% strikeout rate and an elite 23.2% K-BB rate. While the talented left-hander is unlikely to be fully built up as a starter, getting Luzardo back in any capacity would still be a major boost for Philadelphia.--Will Brady
Source: The Athletic - Matt Gelb
Shane McClanahan Will Not Pitch in ALDS


Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:19 PM ET
Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash said that left-hander Shane McClanahan (forearm) is "not in play" for the team's American League Division Series roster, per Marc Topkin of the Tampa Bay Times. McClanahan has been sidelined since early September with left forearm tightness. While Cash did not rule McClanahan out if Tampa Bay advances past the ALDS, it appears the 29-year-old's return is not imminent. Injuries are nothing new for McClanahan, who missed all of 2024 and 2025 due to elbow and triceps issues. He was productive when healthy in 2026, recording a 10-7 record with a 3.36 ERA, 1.12 WHIP, and 106 strikeouts across 118 innings (24 starts). If McClanahan is able to return at some point in October, it seems likely that he would work out of the bullpen rather than attempting to build up as a starter.--Will Brady
Source: Tampa Bay Times - Marc Topkin
Sep 23, 2026, 10:10 PM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (calf) said he intends to be ready for Game 1 of the American League Wild-Card Series, per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. Judge is currently on the 10-day injured list as he battles a calf strain, but it appears he has a chance to be on the field when the Yankees open postseason play next Tuesday. It's been an injury-marred 2026 season for Judge, who was sidelined from late May until early September by a stress fracture in his rib and then immediately went back on the IL with the calf issue. He's also been below his incredibly lofty standard when healthy enough to play, hitting .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI, 45 runs scored, and five stolen bases across 285 plate appearances. Still, getting Judge back would obviously be a massive boost for a Yankees lineup that has largely struggled without its best player.--Will Brady
Source: MLB.com - Bryan Hoch
Ceddanne Rafaela Leaves Early Wednesday With Hamstring Tightness


Keith Hernandez




Sep 23, 2026, 9:05 PM ET
Boston Red Sox outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (hamstring) left Wednesday's game early against the Cleveland Guardians due to tightness in his right hamstring, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Before Rafaela was replaced in center field by Jarren Duran, he went 1-for-1 at the plate in his first game back from a stay on the 10-day injured list this month due to a right-quadriceps injury. The Red Sox initially reported that Rafaela left the game at Fenway Park due to cramping, so hopefully it is nothing serious with the playoffs set to start next week. The 26-year-old's next chance to return to the starting lineup will be for Thursday's series finale against Cleveland. If Rafaela cannot finish out the final week of the 2026 regular season, he could be up in the air for the wild-card series next week against the division-rival New York Yankees. He was an All-Star for the first time this year and came into Wednesday's tilt hitting a nice .282/.317/.443 with a .760 OPS, career-high-tying 16 home runs, 70 RBI, 17 steals, and 67 runs scored across 135 games played and 569 plate appearances in his third full season in the majors.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Dylan Cease Ends his Season on the Injured List


Keith Hernandez




Sep 23, 2026, 8:55 PM ET
The Toronto Blue Jays announced on Wednesday that they placed right-hander Dylan Cease (shoulder) on the 15-day injured list (retroactive to Sept. 20) with inflammation in his right shoulder and recalled right-handers Chase Lee and CJ Van Eyk from Triple-A Buffalo in corresponding moves. With the Blue Jays eliminated from postseason contention, they will shut Cease down for the final week of the regular season. The Blue Jays already announced this week that the 30-year-old All-Star will not need surgery on his shoulder, so he should be ready in plenty of time for spring training next year. Cease really liked pitching north of the border in his first year with the Jays in 2026, as he went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA (league-best 2.55 FIP) and 1.10 WHIP with a career-high 239 strikeouts and 78 walks in 169 innings across 29 starts in his eighth season in the majors. Alex Bregman Not Ready to Return on Wednesday

Sep 23, 2026, 7:22 PM ET
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (face) remains out of the team's starting lineup for Wednesday's game at Wrigley Field against the visiting Miami Marlins, per MLB.com. Pedro Ramirez is making the start at the hot corner and will bat seventh against Marlins right-hander Ryan Gusto. Jackson Holliday Needs Wrist Surgery


Keith Hernandez




Sep 23, 2026, 3:49 PM ET
Baltimore Orioles middle infielder Jackson Holliday (wrist) said he will need surgery to fix his left wrist, either later this week or next week, according to Jake Rill of MLB.com. The good news is that Holliday is not dealing with a complete tear. "Hopefully just go in there and clean it up, and that'll be that," Holliday said. He has been told to expect about a 10-week recovery, so it should not impact his timeline for next season. The 22-year-old was diagnosed with a triangular fibrocartilage complex tear in his wrist. His 2026 season got off to a bad start when he needed surgery to remove a broken hamate bone in his right hand, causing him to get a late start to the campaign. The former first overall pick in 2022 was unable to fully recover, playing in just 98 games for the O's while hitting a disappointing .229/.300/.340 with a .640 OPS, seven home runs, 30 RBI, 45 runs scored, and eight stolen bases in 354 plate appearances. item.content:encoded:
Sep 24, 2026, 11:33 AM ET
Across 102 innings (19 starts) in 2026, Houston Astros right-hander Hunter Brown has recorded a 6-3 record with a 3.26 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 120 strikeouts. The 28-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, missing over two months with a shoulder injury and posting a 4.94 ERA across 27 1/3 innings in July. However, Brown has begun to rediscover his top form in recent outings. Across his last 33 1/3 innings (six starts), Brown is 3-0 with a 2.43 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, and 48 strikeouts. Brown has had issues with command all year long, and his 11.9% walk rate has led to an elevated WHIP. However, he's boosted his strikeout rate all the way up to 28.1% and has struck out 39.1% of the batters he's faced across his first four starts of September. Heading into his final start of the regular season on Saturday against the Athletics, Brown is beginning to look like the fantasy ace he was drafted to be ahead of 2026.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
More Recent News
Sep 24, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Across 501 plate appearances in 2026, Cleveland Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana is hitting .245/.337/.404 with 15 home runs, 57 RBI, 53 runs scored, and 19 stolen bases. The 24-year-old's underlying batted-ball metrics are underwhelming, as he's logged just a 4.8% barrel rate and a 36.2% hard-hit rate. However, Bazzana's 11.2% walk rate is impressive for a young player and helps him get on base consistently and use his speed. Bazzana has also been red-hot of late, hitting .288 with six home runs, 15 RBI, and 11 runs scored across 69 plate appearances in September. If the former top prospect is starting to grow into his power, he could begin to emerge as one of the better second base options for fantasy managers. In leagues where he's on the waiver wire, Bazzana should be a priority target for fantasy managers.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Across 655 plate appearances in 2026, Minnesota Twins first baseman Josh Bell is hitting .255/.317/.416 with 20 home runs, 92 RBI, 76 runs scored, and two stolen bases. The 34-year-old may not have one clear standout skill, but he remains a steady source of power and run production. Bell has kept his strikeout rate manageable at 19.9% while still posting solid barrel (9.5%) and hard-hit (42.0%) rates. The veteran switch-hitter also remains locked into everyday playing time in the heart of the Twins lineup, putting him in a good position to rack up runs and RBI. Heading into the final weekend of the regular season, Bell profiles as a balanced producer for fantasy managers to target on the waiver wire.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Sep 24, 2026, 11:10 AM ET
Across 444 plate appearances in 2026, Baltimore Orioles third baseman/first baseman Coby Mayo is hitting .225/.293/.463 with 24 home runs, 63 RBI, 63 runs scored, and four stolen bases. Swing-and-miss is the obvious red flag in Mayo's profile, as he's struck out in 30.2% of his plate appearances. However, the 24-year-old brings significant power upside with a 13.7% barrel rate and a 47.6% hard-hit rate. Mayo has hit .265 with 12 home runs since the All-Star break, and he's established himself as an everyday presence in the heart of the Baltimore lineup. For fantasy managers in need of power, Mayo profiles as a priority target on the waiver wire heading into the final weekend of the regular season.--Will Brady
Source: RotoBaller
Carlos Lagrange Could Join Yankees' Playoff Roster


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 12:02 AM ET
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that right-handed pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange is "in the conversation" for a spot on the team's postseason roster for the wild-card series next week against the division-rival Boston Red Sox, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. The 23-year-old Dominican is the team's No. 3 prospect at MLB Pipeline, and he has been ramping up his throwing program since coming off the seven-day injured list on Sept. 16 with a sprained right shoulder. Lagrange went 1-4 this year at Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, recording a 4.48 ERA, 1.35 WHIP, and 85:33 K:BB in 64 1/3 innings pitched across 19 appearances (11 starts). If Lagrange is pulled up to the Yankees' playoff roster, he would be making his major-league debut in the postseason in a relief role out of the bullpen. The 6-foot-7, 248-pounder has the tools to excel in high-leverage spots with an upper-90s fastball with armside run and multiple secondary pitches that can generate swings and misses consistently.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
Sep 23, 2026, 11:52 PM ET
Chicago Cubs right-hander Kevin Gausman (shoulder) came up wincing and in some apparent pain after diving to tag a runner out at third base during his start on Wednesday at Wrigley Field against the visiting Miami Marlins, according to Tony Andracki. Gausman was pulled from the game, but he was also at 101 pitches on the night. Manager Craig Counsell said that Gausman's left shoulder got extended awkwardly and "grabbed on him" on the play. He is now sore, and the Cubs will see how he feels in the next couple of days. Gausman is lined up to potentially start Game 1 or 2 next week in the wild-card series in the playoffs. The good news for the Cubs is that the injury is to the veteran's non-throwing arm as well. He came one out shy of a quality start for his fantasy managers on Wednesday, allowing two earned runs on six hits (one homer) while walking one and striking out seven in 5 2/3 frames for a no-decision. The 35-year-old veteran came into his final start of the regular season with a 9-12 record, 4.55 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 177 strikeouts in 172 innings pitched in 2026 with the Cubs and Toronto Blue Jays.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Tony Andracki
Sep 23, 2026, 10:59 PM ET

Volpe has mostly played shortstop in his MLB career, but he recently filled in at second base while Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. was sidelined by a thumb injury. With Chisholm Jr. back, it appears that New York could work Volpe into the mix at third base. The Yankees have gotten underwhelming production at the hot corner from Ryan McMahon, who has hit .210 with 11 home runs across 356 plate appearances in 2026. Volpe's numbers don't appear much better on the surface, as he's hit .244/.321/.335 with two home runs, 26 RBI, 24 runs scored, and 11 stolen bases across 234 plate appearances. However, the 25-year-old has been better in September, hitting .263 with four stolen bases across 40 trips to the plate this month.--Will Brady
Source: Talkin' Yanks
Chase Burns Working on Adding a Sinker


Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:47 PM ET
Cincinnati Reds starting pitcher Chase Burns (groin) was working on a sinker in his final starts before being placed on the 15-day injured list with a groin strain, per Charlie Goldsmith of the Charlie's Chalkboard Substack. Burns put together a dominant season in 2026, recording a 15-3 record with a 2.86 ERA, 1.17 WHIP, and 185 strikeouts across 154 1/3 innings (29 starts). However, Burns threw almost exclusively four-seam fastballs and sliders, mixing in the occasional changeup as well. Burns told Goldsmith that adding the sinker and continuing to develop his changeup should help him go deeper into games. If Burns can successfully add a sinker to his repertoire over the offseason, he could take his production to an even higher level in 2027.--Will Brady
Source: Charlie's Chalkboard - Charlie Goldsmith

Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:36 PM ET
Boston Red Sox left-hander Garrett Crochet (shoulder) will not appear in a regular-season game this week but is still in play to return during the postseason, per Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Crochet is currently on the 60-day injured list and has not pitched since late April due to shoulder and lat issues. While 2026 has been a lost year for the 27-year-old, Crochet was one of the best pitchers in baseball in 2025. Judge is currently on the 10-day injured list as he battles a calf strain, but it appears he has a chance to be on the field when the Yankees open postseason play next Tuesday. It's been an injury-marred 2026 season for Judge, who was sidelined from late May until early September by a stress fracture in his rib and then immediately went back on the IL with the calf issue. He's also been below his incredibly lofty standard when healthy enough to play, hitting .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI, 45 runs scored, and five stolen bases across 285 plate appearances. item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Find the helpers: Checking in with Josh Naylor at the end of year one
item.dc:creator: Kate Preusser
item.description: Last night's walk-off win aside, it hasn't been an ideal first year for Josh Naylor in Seattle after joining the team at the trade deadline last year for a thrilling run to the playoffs, followed up by signing the largest contract of his career this off-season: a contract that represented stability for Naylor, who is on his fourth organization with the Mariners, and a fanbase that was quick to embrace the soft-spoken, cerebral, often enigmatic Canadian. item.content:encoded:
Last night's walk-off win aside, it hasn't been an ideal first year for Josh Naylor in Seattle after joining the team at the trade deadline last year for a thrilling run to the playoffs, followed up by signing the largest contract of his career this off-season: a contract that represented stability for Naylor, who is on his fourth organization with the Mariners, and a fanbase that was quick to embrace the soft-spoken, cerebral, often enigmatic Canadian.
It was, most everyone agreed, a slam-dunk of a deal for both sides: a round peg in a round hole for the Mariners, seeking help at first base; a steady producer at the plate who would balance out some of the Mariners' more volatile strikeout-prone bats; veteran leadership for a young team. And for Naylor, a fast favorite with the fanbase, long(ish)-term stability, a chance to establish some roots in a community and a clubhouse after earning a more permanent place, helping the Mariners to a fairy tale-esque run down the stretch.
Unfortunately, 2026 has been anything but a fairy tale for the Mariners on the field, last night's walk-off aside.
"It was tough as a team this year," admitted Naylor. "We didn't accomplish what we wanted to."
Despite the rough season, Naylor has enjoyed integrating himself in to the Seattle community, both in the clubhouse and beyond. He and his wife Chantel have made a point to explore the state on off-days. They've also attended various Seattle sporting events, especially hockey games, something they're both passionate about and hope to pass on to their young son. Naylor says the family plans to drop in to Seattle this winter to take in some football and hockey, although the family also plans to spend significant time back in Ontario with their son, as Naylor says he wants him to experience the Canadian winters he did as a child.
"I can't wait to get him on skates," he said.
[At this point we should note Naylor's child is not yet one year old. Canadians: Very Serious about their hockey!]
The Naylors have also gotten involved locally with Ronald McDonald House, continuing on the charity work Naylor did with that organization while with Cleveland. Naylor, whose family is deeply important to him, is passionate about supporting families undergoing times of stress.
Maybe because family is so important to him, Naylor has also made a point to put his arms around the younger players, especially his infielders, a responsibility he shares with J.P. Crawford. The two famously took rookie Colt Emerson shopping to buy his first big-league suit, advising on cut and color (lavender!). They also "co-parent" second baseman Cole Young, who maybe doesn't realize exactly how lucky he is to have not one but two veteran players watching over him.
"We sit by each other on the plane," said Naylor. "If we're not talking baseball, we're talking TV shows or video games or whatever. But I try to take him under my wing a little bit. J.P.'s done a great job taking him under his wing, too, and I'm close to J.P., so he's just kind of along for the ride now too."
"We try to spoil him. We take him to the stores and stuff. Spoil him with that. Spoil him with just, like, personal time, me and him and a few other guys. We play video games every night together, and then we just talk about the day. Talk about future of baseball and our future, as individuals. We just became really, really close teammates, which is awesome."
It's a selfless act, to pour so much into another player, so much so that it makes one wonder if Naylor is either mimicking something that was given to him or seeking to avenge something he wasn't given in his career. But he shrugs off the insinuation that this is some kind of karmic scales-balancing.
"I just think it's good to be a good person, regardless of your status or age," he said.
"I just think it's nice to be nice."
Whether it's passing something along or being the change he wants to see, the effect is the same.
"If you can, if you see an opportunity to help, you help. If you need to seek help, seek help. But I don't want to say it's something that was done to me or not done to me. I just think it's it's good to be a good teammate, especially if you know someone is younger than you in experience-wise—not necessarily age, but just game experience—and you see they did something, maybe just get in their ear a little bit, say hey, that was awesome, or hey, you know, maybe try this or that."
"I just try to be a source of confidence for people here. You know, whether it's on a personal level or a
baseball level, I just try to be there for you. If you need me to watch your kids for you because you want to
go out with your wife, I'll watch your kids for you. If you want to have a conversation about baseball and go
back and forth on a topic? I'm more willing to do that. I try to be a really good friend first, and
then an even better teammate after that. That's just my kind of goal in my career and my life."
One thing Naylor has been monitoring is the improvement in his second baseman; he's hopeful Cole Young will win a Gold Glove this year, and credits the work Cole has put in to get him to that level as well as the coaching he's gotten from Perry Hill, or "Bone." Naylor says he doesn't want to speak on behalf of rookie Colt Emerson, but that he knows what it's like to feel the pressure as a rookie in a big-league infield.
"Your first year it's kind of tough because you may not know what to expect, and then the days get harder the worse you do. That's at least what I felt. The days get tough if you're not succeeding, and then you push a little bit harder to succeed, and then you probably fail a little bit more."
"Every young guy goes through it at some point in their career, where you fail and it sucks, and you try a little bit harder the next day and maybe fail a little bit more and then it sucks more, and then you finally succeed and it's like—ah, I didn't need to try so hard for three or four weeks. I was really relaxed today and it worked out."
It's a hard-won mindset Naylor is trying to impart to his young infield-mates, something he says is eased by the daily infield practice mandated by Hill: exposure therapy to reading balls off endless fungo bounces.
"We're all humans, so we make mistakes at times, but being prepared for anything is the mentality," Naylor said, while noting he appreciates the opportunity to watch his fielders – who he says he wants to help win Gold Gloves – improve. "Helping someone get to their best level in life, and then also in their in their field, whether it's sports, whether it's academics, whatever the case is, I think it's super cool to see someone succeed in their in their favorite thing to do."
As much as he likes to see others learn, Naylor considers himself a perpetual student of the game.
"I think you can learn a lot from others. I try to learn a lot from people, whether they're younger or older than me, whether they have five years less than me or five years more than me. I don't really judge them on their time in the game or age. I just judge them on their knowledge. I think knowledge is power, so I try my best to take information from every source I can. Coaches, players, retired players. I like to learn. I think if you have a lot of tools in your toolkit, you'll benefit at the end of the day. If you kind of limit yourself to being like a one-trick pony, it kind of hurts you sometimes. And I've been both. I've been the one-trick pony, and then I had to learn that it's a game of adjustments and a game of kind of maybe doing things different sometimes."
No one can accuse Naylor of being a one-trick pony; he's one base shy of tying his record from last year, an impossible-seeming 30 bags from a slower-footed first baseman. Naylor credits fellow Canadian Dave McKay, the first base coach in Arizona, for teaching him a ton about the mechanics of stealing bases, as well as Mariners first base coach Eric Young Jr. for helping him study pitchers and understand advance scouting to triple his stolen base output for the second consecutive year.
"I just try to find ways to win," said Naylor.
Naylor does not shy from doing what it takes to win. Some of his best accountability partners? His brothers, Bo and Myles.
"I try to improve my whole game every off season. I try to look back at the season—where I failed, what I didn't do as well, and how it can get better, and then God willing, get better. In the off season you have a lot of time to think, you're not really playing the game anymore. So I try to do a lot of thinking with my brothers, and we break down each other's games and talk to each other a lot."
He credits brother Bo with helping him get his swing back over the All-Star Break to where it was over the second half.
"We spent the All Star Break together, and he like broke down everything in my swing. And he said, you know, you need to start going back to this and doing this again and doing that. And he really helped me tremendously. He's a big voice in my career and someone I listen to every day and talk to every day or every other day."
While the off-season is likely coming sooner than anyone had hoped, Naylor is ready to reconnect with the helpers who have helped him, his brothers.
"I look forward to just spending time with them, just discussing baseball while we're watching a TV show or a movie, sitting in our backyard, or I don't know, walking our dogs in the snow. Just chit chatting about how we can get better together. That's something we do every off-season, just try to get better together."
Clearly, Naylor is close with his family, now centralized three time zones away from Seattle, but isn't unhappy about the choice he's made to sign here. For the deep thinker Naylor, the first year is just the beginning.
"I've really enjoyed this organization," said Naylor. "That's why my wife and I chose to be here. Love the guys here. Coaching staff's awesome. City's beautiful. I look forward to kind of getting more comfortable here, and maybe I observed a lot this year just to see how things are ran."
It helps, too, that the fanbase has embraced him so well – something Naylor is appreciative of, especially the fans who shout encouragement when he is struggling ("that doesn't happen everywhere") – and have been freely expressing their creativity in supporting him. Is a bunch of grown men in sailor suits ("Naylor's Sailors") a little weird? Maybe so, but who cares.
"Everyone's weird in their own way. But that's what makes you so beautiful and so perfect for who you are. And if you're not willing to accept it, you're not willing to accept it, that is what it is. But for those who are, I think you get the best out of the person if you're willing to accept who they are. And you have a ton of different personalities in this sport, and in life in general. I think everyone is who they're meant to be."

item.title: [MLB.com] Cómo sutiles ajustes en su postura ayudaron a Acuña a darle un giro a su temporada
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- La mayoría de los jugadores necesita unos días, y quizás hasta un par de semanas, para comenzar a beneficiarse de un ajuste en su swing o en su postura. El venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr. necesitó apenas unas horas.
“En el caso de Ronald, se podía ver de inmediato”, dijo el piloto de los Bravos, Walt Weiss. “Es un atleta fuera de serie, con un talento increíble. Entonces, es un poco diferente. Pero vaya, es muy divertido verlo cuando está encendido de esta manera”.
Lo único que ha frenado a Acuña en las últimas semanas fue la bola de foul que lo obligó a abandonar el juego de la noche del martes con una contusión en la espinilla izquierda. Afortunadamente, las radiografías y una tomografía computarizada no mostraron ninguna fractura. Por lo tanto, el dinámico jardinero podría perderse apenas un par de días.
Acuña llegó al juego de la noche del martes contra los Rojos con el segundo mejor OPS de las Mayores (1.119) desde el 28 de agosto, el día en que ajustó su postura. Su repunte ha aumentado el entusiasmo por lo que podría aportarles a los Bravos, campeones del Este de la Liga Nacional, durante la postemporada.
“Cuando está saludable y entra en una de estas rachas, es uno de los mejores jugadores del béisbol”, dijo el intermedista de los Bravos, Ozzie Albies. “No hay nada más que decir al respecto”.
Acuña estaba lejos de su mejor nivel cuando Weiss decidió dejar al veterano jardinero fuera de la alineación para un partido el 27 de agosto contra los Dodgers. El cinco veces convocado al Juego de Estrellas bateaba .228, con 13 jonrones y OPS de .732 en 81 encuentros de una temporada marcada por dos distensiones distintas en el tendón de la corva izquierdo.
Después de salir del estadio aquella noche, un frustrado Acuña le envió un mensaje de texto al coach de Grandes Ligas de los Bravos, el venezolano Eduardo Pérez, diciéndole que quería realizar prácticas de bateo temprano la tarde siguiente. Fue durante esa sesión que el veterano venezolano se alejó un par de pulgadas del plato, separó los pies unas cuantas pulgadas más y cerró su postura.
La combinación de esos cambios creó una postura muy similar a la que Acuña utilizó durante su temporada de JMV de la Liga Nacional en el 2023.
Acuña lució perdido durante los primeros meses de esta temporada. Además de intentar encontrar una postura cómoda y eficaz, buscaba ganar más confianza en sus dos rodillas operadas. Se rompió el ligamento cruzado anterior de la rodilla derecha en el 2021 y el de la izquierda en el 2024.
Desde el Día Inaugural hasta finales de abril, las dimensiones de la postura de Acuña fueron:
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 31.3 pulgadas (distancia desde la parte frontal del plato hasta el centro de masa del bateador)
Distancia del plato: 25.3 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 31.6 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 34 grados abierta
Vimos la postura abierta durante los Entrenamientos Primaverales y en el Clásico Mundial de Béisbol. Pero su decisión de abrir el lado izquierdo y colocarse más atrás en la caja de bateo no produjo buenos resultados. Conectó dos cuadrangulares y registró OPS de .740 en los 34 juegos que disputó antes de sufrir una distensión en el tendón de la corva izquierdo el 2 de mayo.
Cuando Acuña regresó unas semanas después, cerró su postura (20 grados) y amplió ligeramente la distancia entre sus pies (33.5 pulgadas). Obtuvo algunos resultados alentadores, pero volvió a la lista de lesionados con otra distensión en el tendón de la corva el 10 de junio.
Cuando Acuña regresó nuevamente el 27 de julio, cerró aún más su postura y separó los pies una pulgada adicional.
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 30 pulgadas
Distancia del plato: 25.3 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 34.4 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 14 grados abierta
Aun así, los resultados no aparecieron. Bateó .188, con seis vuelacercas y OPS de .614 en sus primeros 28 juegos tras regresar de la lista de lesionados. Fue entonces cuando Weiss decidió darle descanso a su superestrella para el último juego de la serie contra los Dodgers.
“Si te estoy dando un día libre, probablemente estés teniendo algunas dificultades”, destacó Weiss. “Así que también es un buen momento para tener un día de trabajo. Creo que lo aprovecharon bien”.
Así es como Acuña se ha colocado en la caja de bateo mientras exhibe un nivel digno de un JMV desde el 28 de agosto:
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 29 pulgadas
Distancia del plato: 27.4 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 36.4 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 12 grados
Esto se asemeja mucho más a la postura que utilizó durante su temporada del 2023. A lo largo de la campaña hubo intentos por hacer que volviera a esta postura, caracterizada por una base más amplia y una posición más cerrada. Pero Acuña tuvo dificultades para sentirse cómodo y, al mismo tiempo, mantener la confianza en la estabilidad de sus rodillas.
Postura del 2023:
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 28.8 pulgadas
Distancia del plato: 27.9 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 34.5 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 12 grados abierta
Con esta postura más reciente, Acuña ha bateado .368, con siete bambinazos, uno cada 12.4 turnos al bate, y OPS de 1.107. Su tasa de batazos con el barril ha subido de 12.1% antes del 28 de agosto a 15.5%, mientras que su tasa de swings fallidos ha bajado de 30.1% a 26.5%.
Una gran diferencia ha sido el éxito de Acuña contra las rectas.
Antes del 28 de agosto
vs. recta de cuatro costuras: .119 de promedio (12 hits en 101 turnos), 32.4% de swings fallidos
vs. rectas de cuatro costuras de 95 mph o más: .119 de promedio (7 hits en 59 turnos), 31.8% de swings fallidos
Desde el 28 de agosto
vs. recta de cuatro costuras: .469 (15 hits en 32 turnos), 27.2% de swings fallidos
vs. rectas de cuatro costuras de 95 mph o más: .571 (8 hits en 14 turnos), 34.3% de swings en blanco
“Finalmente encontré mi timing”, dijo Acuña. “Simplemente me estoy divirtiendo ahí afuera”.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Bryce Harper needs to swing less to get better
item.dc:creator: Ethan Witte

item.content:encoded:
The game was 4-1 in favor of the Brewers, but the Phillies had something <ahem> brewing.
On Wednesday night, needing a victory to help lower their magic number by a game, with one out in the seventh inning, Kyle Schwarber was plunked by pitcher DL Hall, followed by an infield single by Trea Turner. The team had done nothing with runners in scoring position all night long, but any chance that they can get with that happening, they would take it. The lineup card stated that Bryce Harper would stride to the plate as it was his turn in the order. What would he do?
August was Harper's best month of the year. His .333/.496/.573 wasn't his top slugging percentage of this season, but as far as actual production on the field, his 194 wRC+ during the month meant he had few peers during that month in terms of offensive production. While the batting average is nice and the slug is perfectly cromulent, if you're like me, it's the fact that he ended up on base half of the time he came to the plate that astounded. That's treading into Bondsian territory.
It also coincided with a new approach that he and the team took: take pitches. A novel concept, it seemed to have been something that eluded the lineup as an offensive approach for many days. Swinging early and often, attacking pitches if they were in the zone, these were the hallmarks of the Phillies lineup these past few playoff years. In 2026, once August hit, it's as though Harper decided that swinging less, particularly chasing less, was what he wanted to do in order to be more productive at the plate.
And whaddaya know, something crazy happened. Once Harper decided to swing/chase less, he actually started to become more productive at the plate.
Now, I'm not saying that it is a direct corollary that swinging less equals more production at the plate. It clearly has to do with more with the fact that he wasn't chasing pitching out of the zone and getting himself out. But it simply cannot be a coincidence. Harper was good this year for most of the year, the usual cold and hot streaks aside, but during August, he was in a god-like mode when hitting. The team started to win more often too and it seemed like the entire offense was hitting well as a result of Harper swinging a hot bat.
However, it is no coincidence that I left the month of September in those charts.
Look at how the things have flip flopped. He's swinging more and has exited that god mode when at the plate. While he's been fine this month (.278/.346/.375 prior to Wednesday), it's mostly just that – fine. The team has needed him to do more, only for him to not be there. I can't help but believe that his sudden change in approach at the plate – swinging more often – has led to a drop in his production.
Anecdotally, it feels like each time Harper is stepping to the plate, particularly with runners on, he is swinging at the first pitch, no matter where it is. If it also feels to you like he is swinging at missing early in the count more and not just at the first pitch specifically, it could be the fact that pitchers have decided to change their pitch mix to him and he is deciding to jump on the first good fastball he sees.
However, the plan has changed against Harper this year.
There has been a noticeable jump in how pitchers are doing the whole fastball/changeup thing while decreasing the amount of breaking pitches he sees. How has Harper fared against this combination?
You guessed it, by swinging and missing at those offspeed pitches more often.
Granted, it's the natural game of cat and mouse that pitchers and hitters have played since the dawn of the baseball age and Harper is caught in the middle of that. He's still getting hits, but a 300 points loss in OPS is an issue.
The first pitch that Harper saw from Hall in that seventh inning, he drilled straight into the plate back to the pitcher for the second out of the game.
If the Phillies are going to do anything in the playoffs, Bryce Harper needs to be productive at the plate. While he did have good months during the season, August showed that a certain approach at the plate was one that worked for him and led to Phillies wins.
As Jack put it in the season three finale of "Lost", we have to go back.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

24 Sep 2026, 18:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Raymond Carlin III)
The Houston Astros keep leaving the door open for the Texas Rangers to win the American League West.
The Rangers keep refusing to walk through.
The Rangers will look to avoid a costly sweep on Thursday afternoon when they face the New York Mets in the finale of a three-game interleague series in Arlington, Texas.
Right-hander Kumar Rocker (5-11, 4.47 ERA) will start for the Rangers against Mets left-hander Zac Thornton (5-5, 3.40).
The Mets dealt another blow to the Rangers' playoff hopes Wednesday night, when former Texas second baseman Marcus Semien hit the tie-breaking homer in the eighth inning of New York's 7-2 victory.
Despite the defeat, the Rangers (78-80) remain tied for first place with the Astros atop the AL West thanks to Houston's 6-5, 10-inning loss to the Seattle Mariners later Wednesday night.
The Rangers also are still in the race for the final AL wild-card berth, trailing the Chicago White Sox by three games.
Thus, the most realistic path to the postseason for the Rangers remains winning the AL West. But Houston won the season series over the Rangers 9-4, which means Texas would need to take the division outright.
The Astros are just 8-12 since Sept. 1 -- a span in which the Rangers have gone 10-10. With a chance to establish themselves as the division favorite over the past two games, Texas has been outscored 13-5 by the Mets (73-85), who have been under .500 since April 11.
'We have to play perfectly the rest of the way,' Rangers first baseman Jake Burger said. 'Obviously, we don't want to be in this situation where we're at now. But we have to go out there and try and get four wins.'
The role of spoiler has become familiar for the Mets, who are 26-19 since trading eight veterans before the Aug. 3 trade deadline. New York has won series in that span over the Rangers as well as the AL East champion Tampa Bay Rays along with the Cleveland Guardians, San Diego Padres and Philadelphia Phillies, all of whom are on the verge of locking up playoff spots.
'That's all we can do right now -- we're not in it, so we want to definitely play our best baseball,' said Semien, who played for the Rangers from 2022 through 2025 and helped them win the World Series in 2023. 'I told the guys we look like we're playing free, and I think that's to our advantage right now.'
Rocker didn't factor into the decision in his most recent start last Friday, when he gave up one run over 4 1/3 innings in the Rangers' 7-1 win over the Toronto Blue Jays.
Thornton earned the victory last Friday after allowing two runs over six innings as the Mets beat the Philadelphia Phillies 6-3.
Rocker has never opposed the Mets, who selected him in the first round of the 2021 draft but did not sign him due to concerns about his shoulder and elbow. He underwent shoulder surgery in September 2021 and was drafted by the Rangers in the first round in 2022 before undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2023.
Thornton has never faced the Rangers.
--Field Level Media

item.dc:creator: Matt Moore
item.description: Good morning, Chicago. ✶ 🔎 Below: Our investigation into the firing of a former principal now running for president of Chicago’s first-ever fully elected school board. 🗞️ Plus: A City Council recap, the push to save a mansion built by Mrs. O’Leary’s son, a new era for Chicago’s candy legacy and more news you need to know. 📝 Keeping score: The Cubs fell to the Marlins, 3-2; the White Sox lost to the Royals, 5-4. 🌤️ Today’s weather: Partly sunny with a high near 68. 📧 Subscribe: Get our morning ne
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, Chicago. ✶
🔎 Below: Our investigation into the firing of a former principal now running for president of Chicago’s first-ever fully elected school board.
🗞️ Plus: A City Council recap, the push to save a mansion built by Mrs. O’Leary’s son, a new era for Chicago’s candy legacy and more news you need to know.
📝 Keeping score: The Cubs fell to the Marlins, 3-2; the White Sox lost to the Royals, 5-4.
🌤️ Today’s weather: Partly sunny with a high near 68.
📧 Subscribe: Get our morning newsletter delivered to your inbox weekday mornings.
⏱️: An 8-minute read
TODAY’S TOP STORY 🔎
Reporting by Mila Koumpilova and Sarah Karp
Biggs banned: Jessica Biggs claims leading a South Side school is a top reason voters should pick her in the race for Chicago’s first elected school board president. That’s even though she was fired from her job as principal of Burke Elementary in 2018, and until recently, was banned from working in Chicago Public Schools.
Candidates’ claims: Biggs, a current school board member, has maintained she was terminated based on a rushed internal investigation after openly criticizing district practices. Her opponents say her dismissal revealed a deliberate, multi-year scheme to falsify attendance data to game her school’s rating.
Our investigation: A WBEZ and Chalkbeat Chicago investigation shows a more nuanced picture. At Biggs’ direction, Burke staff improperly marked students tardy. An uptick in the school’s attendance rate helped improve a high-stakes rating given to the school. But the inspector general’s report does not lay out a full-blown conspiracy to cheat, and it’s hard to say how much of the attendance bump came from mislabeling students versus a concerted effort to get kids to school.
Meet the candidates: Attorney Victor Henderson, leadership consultant Sendhil Revuluri, and former Chicago Teachers Union deputy political director Hilario Dominguez also want the president’s seat. Learn more about them here.
CITY COUNCIL RECAP 🏛️
Reporting by Fran Spielman
Vote delayed: Mayoral allies temporarily derailed an ordinance at Wednesday’s City Council meeting that would require future borrowing to be approved by a three-fifths vote. That’s 30 votes instead of the current benchmark of 26.
Data center decision: Also on Wednesday, Mayor Brandon Johnson followed through on his promise to propose a one-year moratorium on new or expanded data centers until permanent regulations are established to mitigate their impact on the power grid, the water supply and the environment.
TIF approved: Additionally, Council members authorized a $201 million tax increment financing subsidy to pave the way for JDL Development to start construction of the first phase of Foundry Park, a $3 billion replacement for the failed Lincoln Yards mega-project.
Settlements OK’d: A nearly $14 million settlement was approved to compensate two defendants framed by corrupt Chicago Police Detective Reynaldo Guevara for murders they said they didn’t commit. A $6 million payout to the family of a man killed in a police chase was also OK’d.
Meter deal update: On Thursday, a parking meter compromise is up for a vote in the Council’s Finance Committee.
CHICAGO HISTORY ✶
Reporting by Lee Bey
Historic mansion: An endangered Englewood mansion built by the Victorian-era man-about-town and gambler James “Big Jim” O’Leary — his mother and her cow were blamed for starting the Great Chicago Fire — should be granted preliminary landmark status, the city’s two leading preservation groups said Monday.
Key context: The vacant, 125-year-old O’Leary Mansion, 726 W. Garfield Blvd., is currently in demolition court under a raft of code violations. The three-story, 33-room house was designed by Zachary Taylor Davis, an architect whose works include Wrigley Field and the old Comiskey Park.
Status case: “We’re looking at a number of factors [as reasons to landmark the house], from the architecture to the architect, to the people connected with this place,” Landmarks Illinois Interim President and CEO Frank Butterfield said.
MORE NEWS YOU NEED 🗞️
- Funeral home scandal: A hearing is scheduled Thursday in a lawsuit against South Chicago Chapel, the funeral home where 56 decomposing bodies were discovered in August. Here’s what to know.
- 3rd person charged in man’s death: An 18-year-old man appeared in court Wednesday, marking the third suspect charged in the homicide of Kyle Bickham, who was pushed off a Red Line train Sept. 7.
- Tylenol murders lead: A man who died in 1982 could have ties to the Tylenol murders case, according to law enforcement in Idaho. Dr. Matthew Francis Betkouski hasn’t been named a suspect, but his former coworkers reportedly accused him of claiming he could commit the “perfect crime” by slipping poison into pharmaceuticals.
- Misconduct hearing set: The judge who uncovered apparent misconduct by prosecutors in the “Broadview Six” conspiracy case has scheduled a hearing Oct. 1 to help her decide what to do about the discovery that shook the Dirksen Federal Courthouse this summer.
- Chicago extends Divvy contract: The network of rentable bikes, e-bikes and scooters is planning some changes, including discounted pricing on the South and West Sides and a new bike model.
- Joffrey doc: A new PBS documentary captures the discipline, creativity and heart behind the Joffrey Ballet’s trailblazing “Winning Works” program for emerging artists historically excluded from ballet.
ON WBEZ 91.5 FM 📻
- Bridgeport’s concerns: Residents Jonathan Chen and Maria LaGiglio explain how they’re viewing Amtrak’s plan to move its Chicago maintenance facility from South Loop to Bridgeport.
- Card conversations: Jordan Abell, a Chicago high school senior behind a new card game inspiring debate, joins the show to discuss.
- Manopause: Men’s hormones and testosterone levels can change as they age. A medical expert and callers weigh in.
CHICAGO MINI CROSSWORD 🌭
Today’s clue: 3D: Like the cuisine at 88 Marketplace
FROM THE PRESS BOX ⚾🏈🏀
- Remembering Don Cooper: A former White Sox pitching coach who led a World Series-winning rotation, Mr. Cooper died at age 70.
- Bregman recovering: The Cubs’ Alex Bregman said Wednesday that he “felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face,” and he’s working to make a quick return.
- Williams unphased: Bears QB Caleb Williams is back to being a punching bag, but he’s never let a little backlash get him down, writes Jason Lieser.
- High school boys basketball: There have been many changes to high school basketball in the last several years — Joe Henricksen breaks them down.
BRIGHT ONE 🔆
Reporting by Maggie Hennessy
More than a century after Wrigley, Brach’s and Mars helped turn Chicago into a candy epicenter, a trio of artists with an unabashed candy obsession brought their gummy candy startup to the shuttered former Jelly Belly plant in suburban North Chicago, ushering in a new era for this storied city of sweets production.
The actor Martin Starr and musicians and twins Ezra and Adeev Potash cofounded Sweet Stash last fall with an additive-free gummy with the complex flavor and texture dimension of candies they discovered over years of globe-trekking.
“We are obsessed with candy beyond what’s normal and maybe even healthy,” Ezra said.
After months of routinely selling out on Amazon amid requests from retailers for their toothsome, musical note-shaped Jams gummies in flavors like Prickly Pear, Strawbarb and White Peach, the company moved production from Nebraska (the twins’ home state) to Ferrara’s 113-year-old Jelly Belly factory in April.
The move doesn’t just mean taking on bigger orders and getting onto more indie store shelves while maintaining consistency in a product free from gluten, synthetic dyes and corn syrup. This self-starting trio can also keep making candy limited mostly by their imaginations in a city known for confectionery innovation — a rarity for an industry dominated by profit-seeking conglomerates.
“We’re a small band of creative people going up against billion-dollar companies that make candy by the tank,” Adeev said.

item.description: BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak. item.content:encoded:
BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak.
It was just the fifth win in 13 games for the Red Sox, who clinched a playoff spot on Sunday.
The 36-year-old Gray (18-5) is in line to become the fourth Red Sox pitcher since 2000 to lead the AL in victories, joining Rick Porcello (2016), Josh Beckett ('07) and Curt Schilling ('04).
Gray allowed four singles, struck out three, walked one and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
Aroldis Chapman struck out the side in the ninth for his 35th save of the season.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) gave up a run on 10 hits with seven strikeouts.
The Guardians entered with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the AL Central after winning the series opener Tuesday, but needed a win Wednesday combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros to clinch a postseason berth.
The victory came with a price for the Red Sox when center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela left with right hamstring tightness after running out a single the same day he was activated from the injured list. He had been sidelined with a right a quad strain since Sept. 3 and made a diving headlong grab on Steven Kwan, the game's first batter.

item.content:encoded:
Wednesday was Chris Sale's final start of the regular season, so he made the most of it.
Sale was well-rested in his first start since Sept. 11, and it showed. He racked up 10 strikeouts over 5 2/3 innings of one-run ball against the Cincinnati Reds, helping the Atlanta Braves to a 3-2 victory.
The gem raised his season strikeout total to 200, giving him nine career seasons with at least 200 strikeouts. That's the second most by a left-handed pitcher in MLB history, behind only Randy Johnson's 3. It ranks fifth all-time behind Nolan Ryan, Johnson, Roger Clemens and Tom Seaver.
The 37-year-old lefty finishes his 16th Major League season with a 14-9 record, a 2.16 ERA, 200 strikeouts and 5.6 WAR. He also leads MLB in home run rate and K/BB ratio.
With another excellent regular season behind him, the 10-time All-Star now shifts his attention to the postseason. His next start will come in the NLDS next week as he and his teammates begin their pursuit of a World Series title.
More MLB: Brewers Could Be Getting Two-Time All-Star Pitcher Back For Postseason

item.title: [tsn.ca] MLB 2026 playoff intel: Bold predictions, dangerous teams, more
item.dc:creator: Jorge Castillo; Alden Gonzalez; Buster Olney; Jeff Passan; Jesse Rogers
item.description: With less than a week until the 2026 MLB playoffs begin, our baseball insiders have been cultivating their sources and are ready to break down the questions, teams and themes that will shape October -- even before the final 12-team postseason field is set. What is the boldest take we’ve heard from an MLB exec? Is a Los Angeles Dodgers three-peat coming? Can the New York Yankees make a deep run -- with or without Aaron Judge? item.content:encoded:
With less than a week until the 2026 MLB playoffs begin, our baseball insiders have been cultivating their sources and are ready to break down the questions, teams and themes that will shape October -- even before the final 12-team postseason field is set.
What is the boldest take we’ve heard from an MLB exec? Is a Los Angeles Dodgers three-peat coming? Can the New York Yankees make a deep run -- with or without Aaron Judge? And who are the sleeper teams and under-the-radar players to watch?
Here’s the latest intel our MLB experts are hearing as Jeff Passan, Buster Olney, Jesse Rogers, Jorge Castillo and Alden Gonzalez empty their notebooks heading into the playoffs.
What is the boldest prediction you’ve heard from an MLB exec or scout?
Olney: The Padres are going to win the World Series for the first time in their history, with just about everything trending in the right direction. “Once you get into the postseason with all of the built-in off days, that’s going to help their bullpen -- which is the best,” he noted. The Padres’ starting pitching is the team’s biggest concern, but as the Dodgers demonstrated in 2024, you can win with three or four functional starters who are backed by a deep bullpen.
Passan: The Red Sox might be the No. 5 seed, but they’re going to win the American League pennant. Since the All-Star break, one evaluator pointed out, the Red Sox have the best offense in the AL. They’re also an MLB best in Fielding Independent Pitching, a predictive metric that suggests they will continue to throw well. It’s a deep bullpen. It’s a solid-enough rotation. It’s a productive lineup. And, perhaps most helpful of all, it’s the AL, where the path to the World Series is a sandy beach compared to the jungle of the National League.
Do MLB insiders think the Dodgers will turn it on in October again like they did the past two postseasons?
Gonzalez: The general sentiment about the Dodgers seems to be this: They’ll be the favorites until proven otherwise. That’s what they’ve elevated to. They’re too talented, too deep, and they’ve become too adept at navigating seasons to have many detractors, regardless of whatever adversity they might face.
These past couple of weeks have offered a perfect snapshot. The Dodgers’ offense was a serious concern, but now -- with Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez and Kyle Tucker on a heater, and Shohei Ohtani back -- not so much. Their bullpen was, too, but Edwin Diaz has looked sharp since coming back, Roki Sasaki could once again become a weapon and Emmet Sheehan might be too. Regardless, their rotation is widely expected to be an equalizer.
Passan: They’re still the favorites, which is saying something when considering the fatigue that often attaches itself to dynastic teams. But the Dodgers have shown enough vulnerabilities that a number of evaluators believe another team will represent the NL in the World Series. One GM’s sentiment -- “I’d take every NL playoff team over every AL playoff team,” he said -- speaks to the sort of competition the Dodgers will face.
And with so many question marks about how Ohtani and Andy Pages and Blake Snell will fare after returning on the eve of the postseason with no rehab assignments, the Dodgers are not nearly the sure thing they’ve been in recent postseasons. At the same time, they remain, top to bottom, the most talented team in the game, and nobody would be surprised if they win their third consecutive World Series.
How much faith does the industry have in the Rays and Brewers turning the best regular-season records into World Series appearances?
Olney: There is more faith in the Brewers than I’ve ever heard, because the general perception is that they are just a better, deeper team than the group that was bulldozed by the Dodgers in last year’s postseason -- and they’ve got the best starting pitcher, in Jacob Misiorowski. “I think he might hit 107 [mph] in the playoffs,” speculated one evaluator, assessing the impact of the adrenaline, expectations and Misiorowski’s heightened competitiveness. And generally, there is a lot of respect for the Rays, particularly when measured against the low bar of the American League.
Rogers: As much as ever. The Brewers have more believers this year than last simply based on the top of their rotation led by Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. Their depth there is better as well. Robert Gasser has come on strong while rubber-armed Aaron Ashby is a key bullpen guy to go along with Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill.
On the Rays side, their draw for the postseason isn’t perfect -- according to one insider -- but if the Yankees and Red Sox play three games in the wild-card round, it’ll set things up nicely for them in the division series. After that, they’ll be heavy favorites to get to the Fall Classic.
Given Aaron Judge’s health questions, do those in the game think the Yankees will make another deep October run?
Castillo: Opinions vary around the majors. One front office executive said the Yankees have “no chance” of making a World Series run without Judge. Another said he believes it’s possible behind the pitching staff, though the executive added that the bullpen is seemingly running on fumes down the stretch.
Anything can happen in a three-game series. The Red Sox nearly bounced New York last year, falling short in Game 3 thanks to Cam Schlittler’s sterling performance.
After that, the Rays are reminiscent of the Blue Jays club that gave the Yankees trouble last year -- from the regular season through eliminating them in four games in the ALDS. Not having Judge undoubtedly hurts the Yankees’ chances of surviving the gauntlet.
Olney: It wouldn’t be a surprise if they emerge in the American League -- and nor would it be a surprise if they got knocked out in the first round. Without Judge, they are vulnerable against left-handed pitching, and Boston is loaded with lefties.
If they do survive the Red Sox, then they’ll open the division series on the road in the Trop, where they don’t match up well; the Rays’ style of play on their home surface caused all kinds of problems for the Yankees this year.
That all said, the Yankees have the best pitching of the AL teams; they have a good lineup (albeit not great); and their defense has improved.
Who else do MLB insiders feel could be this October’s most dangerous teams?
Rogers: As easy as it would be to pick an AL team to make a surprising run simply because the draw there is softer, experts like the Padres as a dangerous lower-seeded team. They have a good playoff formula now that the rotation has some help and the lineup is hitting for power. In fact, San Diego leads MLB in home runs in September. And of course, they have that vaunted bullpen.
With Aaron Judge on the shelf, the Red Sox are becoming a favorite pick among experts in the AL. Others point to Yankees pitching as their key to advancing. It’s really good behind Cy Young fave Cam Schlittler.
Gonzalez: The Phillies are often a popular pick for this question, and this year it’s no different. They have obvious flaws, from the makeup of their bullpen to their overall defense to, mostly, the status of Jesus Luzardo. But they have a bevy of top-shelf stars, the type that tend to make a major impact on October. They have the experience of having navigated these stakes as a group many times. They have a raucous home environment, one that arguably trumps any in the sport. And, lately, they have Aaron Nola looking like his vintage self.
Still: it’s hard to dismiss the Luzardo factor in all this. He changes everything. “If he’s healthy,” a rival front office executive said, “they’re my answer.” If not, he added, the Brewers are the better, more well-rounded team. Luzardo is that important.
Who are some under-the-radar players with industry buzz as potential postseason stars?
Castillo: Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr., Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers and Padres first baseman Ty France. Mesa, dumped in a trade by the Marlins in February, surfaced from Triple-A in late May to join Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda as dangerous bats. Bauers and France are veterans who lead their respective teams in wRC+ this season -- indicating, at least by that measure, that they’ve been the best hitters on their clubs -- and have been overshadowed.
Passan: In an era when the average fastball is 94.6 mph and pitchers throw it around 30% of the time, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick and Milwaukee right-hander Logan Henderson are anomalies.
Messick, 25, is a favorite of scouts. He throws a four-seamer that averages 94 mph more than 40% of the time, and despite the relative lack of velocity, it’s been a banger of a pitch, the third-most-valuable heater in MLB behind Jacob Misiorowski’s and Cam Schlittler’s.
Henderson leans even more heavily on his fastball (45.7%) even though it’s slower (93.1 mph) and it has the sixth-highest run value.
Why do they work so well? Messick and Henderson both have exceptional control, and as much as velo rules the modern game, there is still room for pitching artistry, and they personify it.

item.title: [tsn.ca] Blue Jays finish season sitting 16th in MLB Power Rankings

item.description: We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
