item.content:encoded:
Mets news: What Marcus Semien said about return to Texas to play Rangers appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Mets second baseman Marcus Semien returned to Globe Life Field on Tuesday for the first time as a visiting player since the Texas Rangers traded him last November. Semien spent four seasons with Texas and helped deliver the franchise's first World Series championship in 2023 after signing a seven-year, $175 million contract before the 2022 season.
The Rangers recognized Semien's accomplishments with a pregame tribute before the Mets opened a three-game series in Arlington. His return carried particular significance because of the role he played during Texas' championship run and the individual honors he collected with the organization.
Before first pitch, Semien opened up about returning to Globe Life Field and reflected on his memorable tenure with the organization. In a post on X, formerly Twitter, MLB.com's Kennedi Landry shared Semien's comments about his return to Texas.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"It's the same drive I've been making for the last four years. There's a lot of memories, a lot of reminiscing," Semien said. "I really think about 2023. It was the pinnacle of my baseball career. … This is a place that's really special."
Marcus Semien returns to Texas.
He said pregame: “It’s the same drive I've been making for the last four years. There’s a lot of memories, a lot of reminiscing.
“I really think about 2023. Or was the pinnacle of my baseball career. …This is a place that's really special.” pic.twitter.com/E0SIsT8uZ7
— kennedi landry (@kennlandry) September 23, 2026
Semien produced one of his best seasons during that 2023 championship run. He played all 162 regular-season games, led the American League with 122 runs and 185 hits, hit 29 home runs and drove in 100 runs. He finished third in AL MVP voting, won a Silver Slugger and later received MLB's Heart & Hustle Award.
The Rangers went on to trade the infielder to the Mets in November 2025 for outfielder Brandon Nimmo, with Texas additionally receiving cash considerations. The move ended Semien's four-year run with the club and sent him to New York with four years left on his contract.
Semien entered Tuesday batting .219 with 14 home runs, 10 stolen bases and a .626 OPS for New York. The Mets came into the series at 71-85 and already eliminated from postseason contention, while the Rangers entered at 78-78 atop the AL West. Texas currently leads New York 3-2 in the top of the sixth inning.
Related: Mets' Marcus Semien shares incredible message on Andy Green's promotion
Related: Mets' Andy Green has the perfect mindset after signing 3-year extension

item.title: [nbcdfw.com] Mets interim manager Andy Green hired for full-time job before season ends
item.dc:creator: Mike Fitzpatrick; The Associated Press
item.description: In a change of direction, the New York Mets hired interim manager Andy Green for the full-time job on Tuesday, giving him a three-year contract. The team made the announcement before starting its final road trip of the year with the opener of a three-game series in Texas against the Rangers. “Over the course of the season, it became evident that the next manager of the New York Mets was already in place,” president of baseball operations David Stearns said in a statement. “Andy has demonstrated
item.content:encoded:
In a change of direction, the New York Mets hired interim manager Andy Green for the full-time job on Tuesday, giving him a three-year contract.
The team made the announcement before starting its final road trip of the year with the opener of a three-game series in Texas against the Rangers.
“Over the course of the season, it became evident that the next manager of the New York Mets was already in place,” president of baseball operations David Stearns said in a statement. “Andy has demonstrated strong leadership qualities and a unique ability to forge connections with our emerging core and distinguished veterans. I look forward to continuing our great partnership as we turn toward the 2027 season.”
Green, who managed the San Diego Padres from 2016-19, had been running New York's farm system before taking over as interim manager when Carlos Mendoza was fired in late June. At the time, Green said he wasn't particularly interested in becoming a permanent skipper again, citing the desire to keep spending time with his three daughters and saying he viewed his interim role on the bench as more of a responsibility to the club than a personal opportunity.
Stearns said Green would return to a front-office role after the season, a stance the executive stuck to in the months that followed — even as the last-place Mets (71-85) improved on the field and several rookies who rose through the minors under Green such as Carson Benge and Nolan McLean flourished in the big leagues as well.
“The players in the clubhouse have rekindled the love I have for being in the dugout," Green said at a pregame news conference in Texas.
And in the end, the Mets committed to Green and chose not to conduct a full search for a new manager this offseason.
“I think Andy is the perfect person for this job,” Stearns said.
“Andy has connected with and pushed our players to perform, despite the disappointment of the season,” Mets owners Steve and Alex Cohen said in the statement. “Over the last several months he has brought discipline, accountability and positivity to the clubhouse, attributes we were seeking in our next manager. ... We are excited for his continued leadership in the dugout.”
Coming into the season, the Mets had high expectations for a franchise without a World Series title since 1986. New York opened the season with baseball’s highest payroll at $358 million and was projected to pay an additional $124 million in luxury tax.
But the Mets underperformed early and were beset by key injuries to Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor and others. They were 34-47 at the midpoint of the season when Mendoza was fired on June 26. The team is 37-38 since Green took over.
“The last three months I think there’s been progress,” Green said. “We’ve got more to do.”
The 49-year-old Green, a former major league infielder, went 274-366 as Padres manager and finished with a losing record in all four seasons. He joined the Mets in 2023 as senior vice president of baseball development and becomes the 26th manager in franchise history.
“I am excited and humbled to officially be named manager of the New York Mets,” Green said in the statement. “When I accepted the interim role, I didn’t anticipate it becoming permanent, but the more time I spent with our players and staff, the clearer it became that this is where my passion and experience could make the greatest impact. That realization led to many conversations with my family, and together we agreed this is the right opportunity at the right time.
"I want to thank Steve and Alex for the love, ambition and commitment with which they lead this organization, and David for the trust he has placed in me. I believe deeply in what we can build together, and I’m honored to continue serving our players, this organization and the amazing Mets fans.”

item.title: [MLB.com] Wheeler llega a los 2,000 ponches en su carrera para guiar triunfo de Filis
item.dc:creator: Todd Zolecki
item.description: El martes por la noche, continuó dejando huella en el partido contra los Cerveceros en el Citizens Bank Park. No solo ponchó a los tres bateadores de la primera entrada, sino que también ponchó a Brice Turang para registrar el número 2,000 de su carrera. Zack Wheeler estableció un récord para los Filis al ponchar a los primeros siete bateadores del encuentro en una victoria por 6-4 sobre los Cerveceros (98-59), superando la marca de Brandon Duckworth de seis ponches seguidos para comenzar un par
item.content:encoded:
El martes por la noche, continuó dejando huella en el partido contra los Cerveceros en el Citizens Bank Park. No solo ponchó a los tres bateadores de la primera entrada, sino que también ponchó a Brice Turang para registrar el número 2,000 de su carrera.
Zack Wheeler estableció un récord para los Filis al ponchar a los primeros siete bateadores del encuentro en una victoria por 6-4 sobre los Cerveceros (98-59), superando la marca de Brandon Duckworth de seis ponches seguidos para comenzar un partido el 5 de agosto del 2002 contra los Dodgers. El ponche de Wheeler en el primer episodio ante Brice Turang fue el número 2,000 de su carrera.
Wheeler es el 96to lanzador en la historia de MLB en alcanzar los 2,000 ponches. Su compañero de equipo, Aaron Nola, llegó a esa misma cifra a principios de esta temporada. Son la segunda pareja de compañeros de equipo que alcanza dicha marca en una misma temporada, los primeros en lograrlo fueron Tim Hudson y Jake Peavy con los Gigantes en 2014.
El lanzador derecho de 36 años fue más allá al ponchar a siete bateadores consecutivos al inicio del juego, superando así el récord anterior de la franquicia de seis ponches, establecido por Brandon Duckworth en 2002.
Fue una salida fantástica contra el mejor equipo en todo el béisbol, un club al que Filadelfia podría enfrentar en la SDLN. Los Filis anotaron tres carreras en la octava entrada contra el bullpen de los Cerveceros para llevarse el triunfo.
Pero Milwaukee fabricó una carrera en el cuarto capítulo para reducir la ventaja de los Filis a 3-1. Sin embargo, en el sexto inning, un sencillo al iniciar la entrada, un boleto con un out, un doble robo y un sencillo con dos outs del venezolano William Contreras anotaron dos carreras para empatar el partido.
Jake Bauers le siguió con otro sencillo con dos outs. Fue el 101er pitcheo de la jornada para Wheeler.
Mattingly dijo antes del juego que esperaba mantener a Wheeler en cerca de 90 lanzamientos, teniendo en cuenta que podría ser su última apertura de la campaña regular. Ahora, el próximo turno de Wheeler en la rotación es el último compromiso de la temporada regular el domingo contra los Rays, pero si los Filis aseguran el Comodín de la Liga Nacional antes del domingo, podría abrir el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines el martes.
Los Filis quieren a Wheeler lo más fresco posible, porque si pretenden ganar esa serie al mejor de tres, casi con certeza será debido a un excelente pitcheo abridor por parte de Wheeler, el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez y otros.
La escuadra de Filadelfia (87-70) terminó el choque con la esperanza de que los Diamondbacks (82-74) cayeran ante los Rockies la noche del martes. Ganando o perdiendo, los Filis todavía podrían asegurar un quinto viaje consecutivo a la postemporada tan pronto como el miércoles.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have just two series left on their MLB schedule before the playoffs begin next week.
Beginning on Tuesday, the Dodgers will play the San Diego Padres, and in the final weekend of the season, LA will take on the Giants.
However, speaking to Tuesday's game, the Dodgers announced a Kyle Tucker lineup decision before their game one with the Padres.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce Emmet Sheehan Demotion Before Padres Series
Kyle Tucker Back in Dodgers Batting Order Hitting 5th
After sitting out for Sunday's game against the Giants, Kyle Tucker is back in the batting order for the Dodgers.
Per @UnderdogMLB, here is the full group:
Dodgers 9/22: "M. Betts SS F. Freeman 1B W. Smith C M. Muncy 3B K. Tucker RF T. Hernández LF J. De Paula DH A. Pages CF T. Edman 2B B. Stewart SP"
Other lineup notes include Josue De Paula getting the nod at DH, Andy Pages being in the lineup after being activated, and Will Smith behind the plate for LA to catch Brock Stewart, who was suddenly announced as the SP for Tuesday's game.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 4 Roster Moves Before Padres Game
Inside Kyle Tucker's Season with the Dodgers
Kyle Tucker is in the middle of his first season with the Dodgers.
It's been a very up-and-down campaign, but Tucker may be hitting a very important stride as October approaches.
He's still batting just .234, but Tucker has 17 home runs now, 70 RBI, and 121 hits over 516 at-bats. His OPS+ is 100, which is exactly league average.
CBSSport.com's RotoWire staff wrote (about Tucker):
"After missing Sunday's series finale against the Giants, Tucker will return to the starting nine for Tuesday's series opener with the Padres. The 29-year-old will bat fifth and man right field for the Dodgers."
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Los Angeles Dodgers Announce Kyle Tucker Decision Before Padres Game appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
피츠버그 파이리츠는 우완 불펜 투수 카밀로 도발을 양도 지명(DFA) 처리했습니다. 과거 올스타이자 내셔널리그 세이브 1위 경력을 가진 그는 트레이드 마감일을 앞두고 유망주 오마르 알폰소와 루이스 크루즈를 내주는 조건으로 양키스에서 영입된 선수였습니다.
피츠버그는 브롱크스(양키스)에서의 부진했던 시기를 털어내고 그의 재능을 되살려보겠다는 프로젝트의 일환으로 도발을 영입했습니다. 피츠버그 소속으로 20경기(19이닝)에 등판한 도발은 평균자책점 3.79를 기록했고 14개의 볼넷을 허용했습니다. 도발이 빠진 활성 로스터의 빈자리는 베테랑 커비 예이츠가 15일짜리 부상자 명단에서 해제되며 채웠습니다.
돈 켈리 피츠버그 감독은 남은 기간 두 차례의 불펜 데이가 남아 있는 상황에서 크리스티안 커티스, 윌버 도텔, 앤드원 켈리 등 많은 이닝을 소화할 수 있는 투수들을 계속 기용하고자 이러한 결정을 내렸다고 설명했습니다.
도발에 대해 켈리 감독은 "그는 정말 훌륭한 경기를 치르기도 했지만 몇 차례 힘든 경기를 겪기도 했습니다"라며, "그는 정말 뛰어난 구위를 가지고 있습니다. 하지만 결국 이 결정은 이닝 소화를 극대화하는 것, 특히 최근에 꽤 좋은 투구를 보여준 젊은 선수들을 활용하는 문제로 귀결되었습니다"라고 밝혔습니다.

item.title: [districtondeck.com] Nationals poach new international scouting director from Astros after scouting misses
item.dc:creator: JJ Phillips
item.description: After a 2025 offseason in which the Washington Nationals overhauled a ton of different things and processes within their organization, the club is back at it again. They hired President of Baseball Operations Paul Toboni to change the infrastructure at all levels, and he has now added another piece to his arsenal of brilliant minds. Nationals poach new international scouting director from Astros The Nationals continue to overhaul the organization's internal workings with another staffing change.
item.content:encoded:
After a 2025 offseason in which the Washington Nationals overhauled a ton of different things and processes within their organization, the club is back at it again. They hired President of Baseball Operations Paul Toboni to change the infrastructure at all levels, and he has now added another piece to his arsenal of brilliant minds.
Nationals poach new international scouting director from Astros
The Nationals continue to overhaul the organization's internal workings with another staffing change. This time, it's the acquisition of director of international scouting Brian Rodgers from the Houston Astros. The Athletic Nationals beat writer Spencer Nusbaum and Astros beat writer Chandler Rome were first with the news.
It's been a turbulent decade for Nationals international scouting. After Johnny DiPuglia took over in 2009, effectively starting from scratch having to clean up the complete mess Jim Bowden left the organization, they saw eventual success with talents like Juan Soto, Víctor Robles (though briefly), and Luis García Jr. That largely dried up later in the 2010s, with the team spending $3.9 million on Yasel Antuna, who crashed out of pro ball in 2023 after failing to produce at any level, in 2017.
In the 2019-20 signing period, the club gave out four bonuses of $600,000 or more to Andry Lara, Pablo Aldonis, Roismar Quintana, and Dawry Martinez. Only Lara ever made it to the big leagues, and while he's still on the 40-man roster, it's hard to imagine he'll maintain that status through 2027 without hitting outright waivers; his brief 9-game relief stint in 2025 was underwhelming, and he's got a 110 ERA- and 102 FIP- (where 100 is average and lower is better) at Rochester this year. Aldonis is still active but hasn't made it past Advanced-A as a 24-year-old. Quintana also never made it past Advanced-A before being released last year, and Martinez never even made it stateside before being cut from the org in 2023.
Other touted international signings since then have been equally underwhelming. Armando Cruz, given $3.9 million in 2021, never hit, and was cut as a 21-year-old last year. The next year, they gave Cristhian Vaquero $4.9 million, and he hasn't progressed past Advanced-A. He's got an 83 wRC+ in the lower minors this year. Nobody in the 2023 class has made any kind of splash in the system either. DiPuglia resigned in September of that year (though he joined the Royals four months later), beginning another period of internal turmoil in the team's international personnel department.
Fausto Severino was promoted from his longtime role as director of Latin American scouting to the international ops director for 2024. While 2024 is recent enough that it's hard to declare the top signing "busts," nobody from that signing class is in MLB Pipeline's Nationals top 30 prospect ranking. Neither Angel Feliz nor Victor Hurtado, the two seven-figure acquisitions, are in FanGraphs' top 45 for the organization. The club did not renew Severino's contract at year's end.
Victor Rodriguez took over as the director of international operations in 2025, overseeing a class that produced Marconi German. That was the only real acquisition that remains of note prior to Mike Rizzo's exit from the organization. Rodriguez remained in that role for the 2026 signing period, however, inking Samil Serrano, who ranked as MLB Pipeline's 26th overall international prospect. He's now the 16th-ranked player in the team's farm system.
Rodriguez will no longer serve in that role going forward, but will remain in the organization, Nusbaum and Rome's piece reports. A period from 2018 to 2024 of almost zero future major league talent being produced severely stunted the Nationals' lower minors, and new director Brian Rodgers is tasked with helping the organization continue to transform itself under the Toboni- and Kilambi-led regime. Rodgers had been Houston's international operations director since 2024, and his top signing of the 2025 international class, Kevin Alvarez, is the club's top-ranked prospect and sits at 77th overall on Pipeline's top 100.
It's one of many top-level changes being made in the Washington organization. Long-tenured director of medical services Harvey Sharman did not have his contract renewed for the 2027 season, Mark Zuckerman reported earlier this month. General manager Ani Kilambi told Nusbaum last week that the team intends to greatly expand its research & development department this offseason as well. It's certainly a new era of Nationals baseball. On this side of things, however, it's likely going to be a few years before we can measure any level of meaningful change.

item.title: [cubbiescrib.com] Former Cubs exec Craig Breslow piggybacks off Chad Tracy's extension with Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Jordan Campbell
item.description: The Chicago Cubs are currently scheduled to play the Boston Red Sox at Fenway Park this weekend to close out the regular season, but the weather forecast could make for an interesting three days. Ahead of that series, the Red Sox took care of a few housecleaning items, including signing manager Chad Tracy to a three-year contract extension. Tracy had been operating with an interim label since replacing Alex Cora in April, but considering the turn-around the Red Sox had this season, it felt like
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Cubs are currently scheduled to play the Boston Red Sox at Fenway Park this weekend to close out the regular season, but the weather forecast could make for an interesting three days. Ahead of that series, the Red Sox took care of a few housecleaning items, including signing manager Chad Tracy to a three-year contract extension.
Tracy had been operating with an interim label since replacing Alex Cora in April, but considering the turn-around the Red Sox had this season, it felt like a foregone conclusion that he would soon get the permanent seal of approval. That wasn't the only move the Red Sox made.
Former Cubs executive Craig Breslow also had his club options exercised by the Red Sox for the 2020 and 2030 seasons. Breslow left the Cubs to take up the top spot in Boston's front office, and had it not been for their turnaround, it would seem that he was headed toward being on the hot seat after the season was over. Instead, he's now aligned with his manager through potentially the 2030 season.
Craig Breslow's journey could hint at what's next for Carter Hawkins
Over the past two years, it seemed that Breslow was putting on a master class of how to lose a fanbase's approval. He ignited tension with Boston's homegrown superstar, Rafael Devers, leading to his trade last year. He then low-balled Alex Bregman in negotiations last offseason, and while that certainly worked out in the Cubs' favor, the impression was that Breslow was in over his head.
Winning cures all, and for Breslow, he's now the unquestioned leader of the Red Sox's front office moving forward.
Breslow's journey could be a tell for what's next for Carter Hawkins and the Cubs. While Breslow never held the GM role with the Cubs, like Hawkins currently does, the impression was that he had finally reached the point where he was ready to run his own baseball team.
For Hawkins, it would seem that he's reached that point. Hawkins is expected to be a candidate for front office vacancies this offseason, and the general consensus is that he's reached the point where he needs his own operation. Hawkins certainly has a nice set-up, working under Jed Hoyer, but this feels like an opportunity where both sides could benefit from the move.
The Cubs would get a new voice in the front office, assuming Hawkins' replacement isn't an internal promotion, and Hawkins would be able to run a team as he sees fit.

item.content:encoded:
Muñoz avoids serious knee injury, could return Tuesday
This browser does not support the video element.
SEATTLE -- Andrés Muñoz has avoided a significant injury to his right knee and could return to the Mariners’ bullpen immediately.
Seattle’s closer underwent an MRI on Tuesday morning, two days after abruptly exiting an outing in Denver with the issue that revealed “nothing serious, nothing structurally concerning,” Mariners general manager Justin Hollander said before the club’s two-game series opener against the Astros.
Muñoz was slated to go through a pregame workout, after which the club would determine if he was available for Tuesday night’s game. He was seen wearing a brace on the knee before players took the field for drills.
Muñoz exited Sunday’s 2-1 win over the Rockies after surrendering a solo homer to Hunter Goodman followed by a five-pitch walk to TJ Rumfield. It was after the walk that he showed more discomfort with the knee.
“It's just something that he's been dealing with off and on a little bit,” Hollander said. “Some hip soreness and knee soreness. So there's not like an event that caused the injury. Just the usual rigors of the season.”
Hollander also provided updates on the rest of the Mariners’ recovering players, in his final state-of-the-IL address before the end of the regular season.
Brendan Donovan (concussion) will not return on this final homestand, meaning that his debut season in Seattle is over. The infielder/outfielder will visit with specialist Dr. Stanley A. Herring at UW Medicine on Wednesday for a followup, and he could begin baseball activities shortly after the season ends, or sooner.
This browser does not support the video element.
In passing on Tuesday, Donovan said that he’s been going through successful ocular therapy and is feeling much better than when he opened up about his debilitating symptoms two weeks ago. At that time, the schedule’s mathematics suggested that a return this season would be a longshot.
Donovan suffered the concussion on Aug. 22 and wound up playing in just 39 games in 2026. Acquired in a splashy three-team trade leading into Spring Training, Donovan remains under club control through next season.
Emerson Hancock’s season could also be over. It’s possible that he’s activated from the 15-day IL and could be available in relief in the coming days, but that will hinge on whether there’s value in doing so, per Hollander. The abductor strain that Hancock suffered in Toronto three weeks ago won’t impact his offseason program.
Also, Matt Brash (right lat strain) recently received a platelet-rich plasma injection while recovering in Arizona. He will be down from his normal offseason program until roughly eight weeks after the season ends.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Recent DFA Could Open Door for SF Giants Reunion With Familiar Reliever
item.dc:creator: Dominic Minchella; Unknown
item.description: The San Francisco Giants are going into a rebuild after trading away several top names at the MLB Trade Deadline, such as Luis Arraez, Heliot Ramos, and Robbie Ray. item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco Giants are going into a rebuild after trading away several top names at the MLB Trade Deadline, such as Luis Arraez, Heliot Ramos, and Robbie Ray. But with every rebuild, there's always a possibility for a familiar face to get a second chance with the franchise, depending on specific needs.
It's clear the Giants bullpen is one of those specific needs, holding a bullpen ERA of 4.18 and only collecting 30 saves this season. With many young pitchers looking to pave their path into the bullpen, this club needs a veteran reliever that it can rely on.
Across the league, the Pittsburgh Pirates announced Tuesday afternoon that they've designated former San Francisco Giants closer Camilo Doval for assignment as a corresponding move to activate Kirby Yates off the injured list.
Isn't that crazy how the world of baseball works? Doval spent his best years as a member of the Giants organization, holding a 3.29 ERA in 275 games for the franchise from 2021 to 2025, when he was traded to the New York Yankees. As a Giant, Doval collected 107 saves. Elsewhere, between the Yankees and the Pirates, Doval has recorded two saves.
Should the Giants Reunite with Doval?
This season, Doval holds a 4.30 ERA and a 1.52 WHIP with New York and Pittsburgh, having pitched well with the Pirates, but not well enough for the team to keep him around. Pirates manager Don Kelly had a blunt statement about Doval that the Giants know well.
“He had some really good games and a couple tough ones,” Kelly said via Aiden Stepansky of MLB.com. “He's got some really good stuff, and ultimately, it really just came down to being able to maximize innings.
It's not like Doval has lost all of what made him an All-Star in 2023, but he hasn't been that pitcher since. However, having tested the waters away from San Francisco, and then the Giants testing the waters without Doval, perhaps it's a reunion that has to happen.
Doval seemed to have figured it out the first month he was in Pittsburgh, pitching to a 2.84 ERA in August. But in September, it's been a different story, in which he's posted a 5.68 ERA in 6.1 innings across seven games.
Bringing Doval back to a franchise where he has previously felt comfortable and confident could be beneficial. As a veteran closer, he has the opportunity to mentor the younger players, while learning from them as well. San Francisco might be making the right choice by following the path that seems laid out before them.
According to MLB's DFA rules, within seven days of the transaction, the player can either be traded or placed on outright or unconditional release waivers. So, the Giants could be a team to watch for the next few days to see if they're a fit for their former reliever again.
Dominic Minchella is a 2024 Eastern Michigan University graduate with a BA in Communications, Media, and Theatre Arts and a Journalism minor. He covers Major League Baseball for On SI and spends his free time watching games and sharing his insights.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Yankees Face Judge Dread
item.dc:creator: Michael Baumann
item.description: When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

item.content:encoded:
Ronald Acuña Jr. was unable to finish Tuesday's game against the Cincinnati Reds.
In the bottom of the third inning, the Atlanta Braves star fouled off a pitch that struck the inside of his left leg.
The outfielder looked like he was trying to walk it off, but he couldn't get past it and went down on the field. A trainer came out, and it looked like Acuña was in a lot of pain. He left the field, was pulled from the game, and was replaced by Brewer Hicklen.
Acuña missed time earlier this season due to a hamstring strain. He initially sustained the injury in May and then aggravated it again in early June. This caused him to miss more than a month and a half of action, and he didn't return until July 27.
The good news is that the Braves have already clinched both a postseason berth and the National League East title. The bad news is that if this injury is serious enough that Acuña needs to be added to the IL, any stint would affect his availability for Atlanta's first playoff series.
If Acuña is indeed sidelined for part of the Braves' playoff run, it would not be the first time he has missed out. The outfielder tore his right ACL in July 2021, months before the Braves went on to win the World Series over the Houston Astros.
The 28-year-old is the face of Atlanta's lineup, serving as the leadoff hitter. This season, he has played in 103 games and is slashing /.260/.352/.463 with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, and 20 stolen bases.
Acuña is three years removed from a dominant 2023 campaign where he tallied 41 home runs and 73 stolen bases for the first 40-70 season in MLB history.
The Braves have five more regular season games before the playoffs begin next week. If Acuña is sidelined, Atlanta will have to shuffle around its lineup, likely playing catchers Drake Baldwin and Sean Murphy in the same lineup with one as the DH. This would free up Mike Yastrzemski to take over in right field, but the Braves could also go with Hicklen or Dominic Smith as well.

item.dc:creator: Dan Martin
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge is out, and the Yankees don’t know when — or if — he’ll be back.
So if they’re going to go anywhere in the playoffs, they’ll almost certainly have to do some work without him.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
That means Cody Bellinger’s role will be even more important than it’s been for much of the season, and lately, he’s answered the call.
It was Bellinger’s two-run shot in Game 1 on Tuesday that provided all the scoring in the 2-0 win over Tampa Bay in The Bronx.
The blast was Bellinger’s 17th of the season and fifth in his past 12 games.
With Judge out indefinitely with a strained right calf, Aaron Boone said the team was “not expecting” Judge to be available for the wild-card series that begins next week.
As Bellinger said following the win in Tuesday’s opener, any chance the Yankees have without Judge will be due to a collective effort.
But there’s little doubt that Bellinger — whose $36.5 million salary this year is second only to Judge’s $40 million — will be called upon more than most.
Against right-hander Nick Martinez of Tampa Bay, Bellinger hit second — a spot that he and Ben Rice have mostly split in Judge’s absence.
Rice doubled off Martinez to lead off the bottom of the fourth of a scoreless game, and Bellinger followed with his shot out to right.
“[Rice] had a great at-bat in front of me [and] saw a lot of pitches,’’ Bellinger said. “It was a close game. I’m not trying to do too much at all. I want to keep it really simple, put a good swing on the ball.”
It’s the approach the Yankees are hoping to have without Judge, whose “moderate” strain has put their October plans in jeopardy.
“I think for us, it’s one game at a time,’’ Bellinger said. “We all believe in each other in this locker room. We’re not looking too far ahead.”
But it’s hard not to wonder how the lineup — and team — will withstand another Judge absence.
“Having Judge on our team helps us tremendously,’’ Bellinger said. “We’ve just got to continue to come out and win games, playing for each other, leaning on each other [and] playing good baseball.”
As the Yankees have noted, they’ve stayed in the postseason picture, even as Judge missed three-plus months with a fractured rib this summer.
Shop Yankees Merch
“We have a lot of talent in this locker room, a lot of depth,” Bellinger said. “A lot of different guys stepped up, whether it’s their first year in the big leagues or getting traded [here]. We keep playing winning baseball.”
Bellinger added to that not just with his bat Tuesday, but with his arm, as well.
After Victor Mesa Jr. opened the sixth with a single off Carlos Rodón, Bellinger started an inning-ending double play two batters later when Richie Palacios lined out to left.
Mesa didn’t know where the ball was and didn’t get back to first in time to beat Bellinger’s strong throw.
“He went through that stretch when he was struggling and then got injured,’’ Boone said of Bellinger’s earlier slump and hamstring injury. “But he’s dialed in now and hitting line drives all over the ballpark. … It’s good to see as we get down the stretch.”

item.title: [MLB.com] Bregman (facial fractures) won't need IL, could return this weekend

item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO -- If Alex Bregman is not spotted in the Cubs’ locker room before a game, chances are he is down the tunnel in the batting cage. That was no different on Tuesday afternoon, even with his left cheek and eye still bruised and swollen from the foul ball that struck him in the on-deck circle on Sunday in Cincinnati.
“He’s completely himself,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said. “He can’t sit still. He’s all over the room. Those are really good signs.”
All the worst-case scenarios that immediately came to mind for anyone who witnessed Sunday’s freak accident have, by all accounts, been avoided. Bregman has had multiple appointments with a variety of specialists and has received positive news on all fronts. His vision is fine. There are multiple fractures in his cheek area, but no surgery is required.
Counsell noted prior to Tuesday’s game against the Marlins that Bregman would not be placed on the injured list and a return before the end of the regular season has not been ruled out. In the coming days, Bregman will continue to ramp up his activity to gauge whether any symptoms arise, and the Cubs’ medical and training staff will assess and proceed from there.
“I think Alex is going to be fine, I really do,” Counsell said. “He’s planning on playing. He knew he had to get some good news from the doctors. He got that good news. So he’s going to do everything in his power. And as long as symptoms don’t increase, or happen as he increases activity, I think you’re going to see him play.”
After this three-game series at home against the Marlins, the Cubs are scheduled to play three games against the Red Sox in Boston, where Bregman played last season. The North Siders headed into Tuesday atop the National League Wild Card standings.
In the fourth inning of Sunday’s 9-1 win over the Reds, Michael Busch checked his swing and fouled off a pitch from Cincinnati’s Luis Mey. The baseball hit the dirt and then struck Bregman in the face as he prepared to hit. The third baseman immediately dropped his bat, grabbed his face and headed down the dugout steps with members of Chicago’s staff.
Bregman was examined at a local hospital and cleared of any concussion symptoms. He posted photos on his Instagram account that showed severe swelling around his eye, but declared, “I’ll be back.” The Cubs had a staffer remain in Cincinnati to drive back to Chicago with Bregman, as opposed to having him fly back with the team.
“He doesn’t look great, that’s for sure,” Cubs president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer joked. “But no one loves to play more than him. I can say that with no equivocation. I’ve never had a player that loves baseball as much as he does. He just wants to play all the time. Right away, when we first heard from him afterwards, [he said] he was going to find a way to do it.
“There were scenarios where there was no way it was going to happen -- if he needed surgery or things like that. But he didn’t. Now he has the chance to get out there. And there’s nothing he wants to do more. It’s impressive.”
During the pregame hours on Tuesday, Bregman got a workout in and also donned a helmet and headed into the batting cage to track pitches on the high-velocity Trajekt machine. Around the clubhouse and in the cage, Bregman was very much acting like his usual self, which brought a smile to Nico Hoerner’s face.
“His reaction to everything has been uplifting,” Hoerner said. “Just in being relentlessly aggressive and positive and speaking about all the things he’s excited to do and turn it into. Just his own mentality kind of leads the group in that way in how to handle it. It was a super jarring thing and terrible timing, obviously.”
Through 153 games this season, the 32-year-old Bregman has hit .262 with 26 homers, 32 doubles, 89 RBIs and an .804 OPS. Since the All-Star break, however, only teammate Pete Crow-Armstrong (4.5) has been worth more wins above replacement (per FanGraphs) in the Majors than Bregman (3.4). The third baseman has hit .296 with 17 homers, 17 doubles, 48 RBIs and a .978 OPS in 59 games in the second half.
While Bregman is out, the Cubs have both Pedro Ramírez and Matt Shaw as options for third base. Ramírez -- recently the primary starter at second base, while Hoerner manned short with Dansby Swanson on the IL -- was in the lineup on Tuesday night. Shaw was Chicago’s main third baseman last year before Bregman came aboard via his five-year, $175 million deal.
“No one’s asking anyone to replace Breggy and what he’s done this year,” Hoerner said. “But in the meantime, we’re very well-equipped to handle it.”

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Ronald Acuña Jr. was forced to exit Tuesday night’s game against the Reds at Truist Park after fouling a pitch off his lower left leg in the bottom of the third inning. The Braves later announced he had suffered a left shin contusion, but that X-rays were negative.
Acuña fell to the ground in pain immediately after the foul ball hit just between his left shin guard and left knee. He tried to take a few steps before going to the ground again.
The Braves' outfielder was able to get to the dugout under his own power.
Acuña entered Tuesday tied with Alex Bregman for MLB’s second-best OPS (1.119) dating back to Aug. 28.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Why Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber Are Key to Phillies Playoff Success
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Teape; Unknown
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies have a little bit of work left to do to secure a playoff spot in the National League. With six games remaining in the regular season, the Phillies hold a four-game lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks. But because they do not possess the tiebreaker, Philadelphia still has a Magic Number of three. item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies have a little bit of work left to do to secure a playoff spot in the National League.
With six games remaining in the regular season, the Phillies hold a four-game lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks. But because they do not possess the tiebreaker, Philadelphia still has a Magic Number of three.
Over the next six games, they need some combination of three victories of their own and losses by the Diamondbacks. They are heavily favored to make the postseason field, but then will be jostling for seeding with the Chicago Cubs, who are currently the No. 1 Wild Card team, and the San Diego Padres, who are currently No. 2.
To catch those teams and make any noise in the playoffs, the Phillies are going to need their stars to play up to their capabilities. Two players they will be counting on to produce are right fielder Bryce Harper and designated hitter Kyle Schwarber.
Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber have been elite against fastballs
In the playoffs, there is a little extra juice when facing opponents. Pitchers are throwing the ball a little harder, and handling velocity becomes a key component for a team to find success. Luckily for Philadelphia, their two star sluggers are among the best in baseball when facing heat.
Some of the nastiest offerings in baseball are off-speed and breaking pitches that can play up a four-seam fastball. So, when a batter gets the opportunity to jump one of those fastballs, they need to make it count.
Harper and Schwarber both accomplish that. As shared by David Adler of MLB.com, thus far in 2026, they are two of the most productive players in the MLB against fastballs. Schwarber is second in the MLB with a batting run value of +30 runs created, which trails only Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros, who has +32.
The Phillies slugger has launched 27 home runs against fastballs this season, which is the most in the MLB. Harper has hit 18 home runs when facing fastballs, and his +28 runs created is the third most in baseball. Willson Contreras of the Boston Red Sox and Ben Rice of the New York Yankees round out the top five with +25 and +23 runs created apiece.
Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber produce under brightest lights
While the Philadelphia duo has succeeded against that pitch type, they have also gotten the job done even when the pitcher is throwing with elite velocity. When facing fastballs that are 97 mph or faster this season, Harper has a slugging percentage of .523 with three long balls.
Schwarber has been slightly better, with a .525 slugging percentage and six home runs, which once again leads the MLB.
Even more encouraging for the Phillies is that since the two became teammates, their production against fastballs is even better in the playoffs. Harper has an eye-popping .778 slugging percentage with eight home runs since 2022, making him the best fastball hitter in the MLB postseason during that span.
Schwarber has 10 home runs in the playoffs with a .722 slugging percentage. Hopefully, they keep that production up to help Philadelphia advance in the postseason.

Kenneth Teape is an alumnus of SUNY Old Westbury and graduated in 2013 with an Honors Degree in Media Communications with a focus on print journalism. During his time at Old Westbury, he worked for the school newspaper and several online publications, such as Knicks Now, the official website of the New York Knicks, and a self-made website with fellow students, Gotham City Sports News. He was a contributor to HoopsHabit, with work featured on Bleacher Report and Yardbarker. In addition to his work here, he is a reporter for both NBA Analysis Network and NFL Analysis Network, as well as a writer and editor for Packers Coverage. item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Zack Wheeler opens with Phillies record 7 straight strikeouts, hits 2,000 for career
item.dc:creator: Kristie Ackert; USA TODAY
item.description: Zack Wheeler walked out to the mound at Citizens Bank Park Tuesday night needing three strikeouts to reach 2,000. It took him 12 pitches. Garrett Mitchell went down first. Then Jackson Chourio and Brice Turang were rung up as Wheeler reached the milestone against the Milwaukee Brewers. But, Wheeler kept going. William Contreras, Jake Bauers and Christian Yelich struck out in the second. Luis Lara struck out to lead off the third inning. Wheeler struck out seven straight Brewers to start the game
item.content:encoded:
Zack Wheeler walked out to the mound at Citizens Bank Park Tuesday night needing three strikeouts to reach 2,000. It took him 12 pitches. Garrett Mitchell went down first. Then Jackson Chourio and Brice Turang were rung up as Wheeler reached the milestone against the Milwaukee Brewers.
But, Wheeler kept going.
William Contreras, Jake Bauers and Christian Yelich struck out in the second. Luis Lara struck out to lead off the third inning. Wheeler struck out seven straight Brewers to start the game, something no Phillies pitcher had done to start a game. Cooper Pratt finally ended it by grounding out to third.
Wheeler, 36, is the 96th pitcher in major league history to reach 2,000 strikeouts and only nine got there faster.
It came almost a year after a surgeon in St. Louis removed his top rib to address the circulation problem in his arm.
The trouble started after a start in Washington on Aug. 15, 2025. Wheeler felt some heaviness in his right shoulder. By the next morning doctors had found a blood clot near it. The diagnosis was venous thoracic outlet syndrome, meaning a vein was getting pinched between his collarbone and rib cage. The fix was taking out the first rib and some of the muscle around it. He missed the rest of the season and the playoffs.
He came back April 25 against Atlanta, capped at 90 pitches. He hasn't looked back. Wheeler entered Tuesday 13-5 with a 2.99 ERA and 177 strikeouts in 150½ innings. In his previous four starts he had allowed three runs in 26 innings.
Aaron Nola still owns the Phillies' mark for strikeouts in a row at any point in a game. He struck out 10 straight Mets in June 2021, matching Tom Seaver's major league record from 1970. The modern record for starting a game that way is nine, set by Miami's Pablo Lopez against Atlanta in 2021.
Wheeler finished with 11 strikeouts Tuesday night in 5⅔ innings.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Zack Wheeler opens with Phillies record 7 straight strikeouts, hits 2,000 for career

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Alex Bregman injury update shows how he has changed the Chicago Cubs
item.dc:creator: Gavin Groe
item.description: Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman suffered multiple fractures in his face after being struck inadvertently by a foul ball this past Sunday during a game against the Cincinnati Reds. The injury occurred in the top of the fourth inning while Bregman was standing in the on-deck circle. Cubs first baseman Michael Busch checked his swing and the ball immediately struck Bregman. He was removed from the game and hospitalized as he underwent imaging to confirm the severity of his injuries. Bregman
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman suffered multiple fractures in his face after being struck inadvertently by a foul ball this past Sunday during a game against the Cincinnati Reds. The injury occurred in the top of the fourth inning while Bregman was standing in the on-deck circle. Cubs first baseman Michael Busch checked his swing and the ball immediately struck Bregman.
He was removed from the game and hospitalized as he underwent imaging to confirm the severity of his injuries. Bregman also shared graphic images of the injury which worried Cubs fans given how swollen his face was and how close the MLB postseason is.
However, manager Craig Counsell had an encouraging update when speaking with reporters ahead of Tuesday's game against the Miami Marlins.
Counsell shared that not only would Bregman avoid the injured list entirely, but there is a chance he even returns before the end of the regular season. He even took part in strength work and tracked pitches from a machine, officially resuming baseball activities.
What Alex Bregman Has Meant to the Chicago Cubs
Bregman's decision to push through the discomfort speaks volumes about his character and what he has brought to this Cubs team. Bregman signed this past offseason to a five-year, $175 million deal, which was quite the investment for an aging infielder whose prime may be behind him. However, one of the main reasons Chicago made the move was for his veteran presence and ability to lead by example.
Everywhere Bregman has played in his career, teams win. In Houston he won a World Series title, and with the Red Sox last year he helped take them to the MLB playoffs, guiding a young team not just with his bat but with his toughness and leadership.
National League MVP frontrunner Pete Crow-Armstrong has even credited Bregman for his success this year and for being in his corner throughout the season.
Sep 18, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (3) waits on deck to bat before the game against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. Mandatory Credit: Aaron Doster-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
For the Cubs, Bregman being available will improve their playoff chances on the field. But his addition to the clubhouse in general has been invaluable. The Cubs are on the verge of punching their ticket to the postseason, and Bregman will be along for the ride.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Blue Jays Receive Encouraging News About Dylan Cease's Injury
item.dc:creator: Maanav Gupta; Unknown
item.description: Injuries have started to take a toll on the Toronto Blue Jays lately. While it seemed like there was still hope for Toronto to make the postseason a couple of weeks ago, that has ultimately not turned out to be the case. The struggles have been real, and the injuries have not made it easier. Outfielder Brett Bateman suffered a hip injury on Monday night, while first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has dealt with back tightness. Not to mention starter Trey Yesavage, who just returned from knee surg
item.content:encoded:
Injuries have started to take a toll on the Toronto Blue Jays lately. While it seemed like there was still hope for Toronto to make the postseason a couple of weeks ago, that has ultimately not turned out to be the case.
The struggles have been real, and the injuries have not made it easier. Outfielder Brett Bateman suffered a hip injury on Monday night, while first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has dealt with back tightness. Not to mention starter Trey Yesavage, who just returned from knee surgery after six weeks.
Ace Dylan Cease had been holding down the rotation recently, but even he hasn't been immune to the injury bug that has hurt the Blue Jays this season. Cease has been a lifeline to Toronto's pitching staff, but had been dealing with shoulder fatigue over the past few weeks, according to manager John Schneider.
Cease struggled mightily against the Texas Rangers on Friday, going just 2.2 innings and walking six, while giving up four runs (one earned). He went back to Toronto for an MRI and was scratched from his next start on Wednesday.
It was revealed on Monday that the MRI only showed inflammation in the right shoulder and no structural issues. Cease will not need surgery for anything more serious.
More on Cease's Injury Situation
The 30-year-old explained the news himself and the fact that he's just been diagnosed with shoulder inflammation. This isn't an issue that is expected to go into 2027 and affect his availability for next season.
It's still unlikely that Cease ends up pitching again this season with less than a week left, although that's still being determined. Given the Jays are basically out of postseason contention, there's really no need to push him.
The shoulder issue is what caused Cease's pitch velocity to go down.
“The velocity being down has been a little bit concerning,” Cease said, according to Keegan Matheson of MLB.com. "But at the same time, I’m getting outs. It wasn’t anything that was too scary because nothing about it feels like I’ve got something that needs surgery."
After his incredible complete game at the Boston Red Sox on July 25, where he threw 120 pitches, Cease didn't look as strong, even though he still ended up throwing six quality starts from that time until now.
“It’s definitely a bit heavy and achy, just not normal,” Cease said. "The last couple of starts, the velo keeps going down and down. Especially that last one, I almost felt like I was hurting the team."
It's clear that the issue caught him to him, but the fact that he pitched through it at a high level for some time shows the quality of Cease.
He has posted a 2.40 ERA in 29 starts, which is the second-lowest mark in the American League. Cease has a career-high 239 strikeouts in 169 innings pitched, with an 11-6 record.
Maanav Gupta primarily covers Houston sports for On SI. He graduated from the University of Houston in the summer of 2025 with his bachelor’s in journalism and a minor in Spanish. Gupta spent three years at the student newspaper, The Daily Cougar, and also covered the 2025 Final Four and National Championship. He also has his own YouTube channel, Maanav’s Sports Talk, where he has interviewed professional athletes and broadcasters like Jose Altuve, Jeremy Peña, J.J. Watt, and Jim Nantz. Gupta has been writing about the Astros for various publications since 2024. You can find Gupta on X, Instagram and TikTok @MGSportsTalk.

item.title: [phillyvoice.com] The Phillies aren't serious
item.dc:creator: Nick Tricome PhillyVoice Staff
item.description: September 22, 2026 The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back. But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go. Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full. item.content:encoded:
September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Red Sox might've cemented Craig Breslow’s rise off the hot seat too soon
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years. With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. item.content:encoded:
The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.
